senses.definition: (rare) One who abnegates, denies, or rejects.
senses.example: The abnegator refused every luxury offered to him, even the warm meals his parishioners brought.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A person who renounces, denies, or gives up something, such as a right, a claim, or a pleasure.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on AB, and the final syllable is an American r-colored 'er' sound. Non-native speakers often stress the wrong syllable or pronounce the last syllable as a full 'tor.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to admirable. It names someone who gives up something, which can be seen as noble or self-denying depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Abnegator is rare and mostly appears in formal writing or literary analysis. Americans seldom use it in speech. For everyday talk, you would say someone who gave something up or who refused a privilege.

distinctions.note: An ascetic lives a life of deliberate austerity as a whole. An abnegator may give up a specific right or claim without living an austere lifestyle.
Renouncer is a more general and more common word for someone who gives up a position, belief, or possession. Abnegator is more formal and focuses on the denial of self.

examples.professional: As an abnegator of executive privilege, the director insisted the team own the roadmap.
examples.analytical: The abnegator in the novel becomes a kind of moral mirror, exposing the self-interest of those who claim the same rights.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who hands back the keys to a car they could still drive.
nuance.etymology: Formed from abnegate plus the agent suffix -or, from Latin -ator, 'one who does'.
common_mistakes: Using abnegator for the act itself; the act is abnegation.
Confusing it with negator or negotiator, which have different meanings.
Forgetting the r-colored final syllable, which should sound like 'er' in American English.

senses.definition: Fully sufficient; found in copious supply; in great quantity; overflowing.
senses.example: Blackberries are abundant in this part of the country in October, so we always make lots of jam.

senses.definition: Richly supplied; wealthy; possessing in great quantity.
senses.example: The hillside was abundant with wildflowers after the unusually wet spring.

senses.definition: Being an abundant number, i.e. less than the sum of all of its divisors except itself.
senses.example: In number theory, twelve is abundant because its proper divisors sum to more than twelve.

core.definition: Existing or available in large amounts, more than enough; plentiful.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -BUN-, with a short 'u' as in 'cup.' The last two syllables are reduced, so 'dunt' sounds like 'dent' with a weak vowel. Avoid saying 'ah-bun-DANT.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests generosity, sufficiency, or richness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'abundant' in writing, speeches, and formal descriptions, such as 'abundant rain' or 'abundant parking.' In casual speech they more often say 'plenty of' or 'lots of.' The adjective is often followed by 'in' with a noun, as in 'abundant in resources.'

distinctions.note: 'Plenty' is the everyday, informal word, while 'abundant' sounds more formal and written.
'Ample' means enough or more than enough and often refers to space or time, while 'abundant' stresses a large quantity.
'Copious' is more formal and often describes things like notes, rain, or flowing liquids.

examples.everyday: There's abundant parking at the mall on Sundays, so we don't have to worry about it.
examples.professional: We have abundant data for the churn model, so sample size shouldn't be the constraint.
examples.analytical: The manuscript offers abundant evidence that the early church read these letters as authoritative.

nuance.analogy: Like a well that never runs dry, no matter how much water is drawn from it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin abundare 'to overflow,' from ab 'from' and undare 'to surge,' from unda 'wave.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable (uh-bun-DANT) instead of the second.
Writing 'abundant of' instead of 'abundant in' or simply using the noun 'abundance of.'
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture 'abundant' translates Greek words meaning overflowing or superabundant, from perisseuō 'to abound, overflow.' John 10:10 says Jesus came that people may have life and have it abundantly, a verse often read as the fullness of life in him. Romans 5:20 says that where sin increased, grace abounded all the more, and 2 Corinthians 9:8 says God is able to make all grace abound toward believers.

senses.definition: The quality of being acceptable; acceptableness.

Operation plan review criterion. The determination as to whether the contemplated course of action is worth the cost in manpower, materiel, and time involved; is consistent with the law of war; and is militarily and politically supportable. (JP 1-02 Department of Defense Dictionary of Military and Associated Terms)
senses.example: The acceptability review examined whether the strike was consistent with the law of war.

core.definition: The quality of being good enough, reasonable, or suitable to be allowed or approved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BIL, the third syllable, and the final -ity sounds like tee. The first syllable is a weak uhk, not ak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes whether something is allowable, and it sounds formal or official.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use acceptability in formal writing, policy, business, and technical reviews. In everyday talk they ask is it okay or is that acceptable instead. In military or policy writing it can mean a course of action is worth its costs, legal, and politically supportable, so check the context. Using it in casual conversation can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Acceptance is receiving or agreeing to something, while acceptability is whether it meets a standard of being allowable.
Feasibility asks whether something can be done, while acceptability asks whether it will be allowed or approved.
Suitability means fitness for a purpose, while acceptability focuses on approval by others.

examples.everyday: Before we build the fence, we should check the acceptability of the height with the homeowners' association.
examples.professional: Before the launch, the product team measured customer acceptability of the new checkout flow.
examples.analytical: Mill argued that the acceptability of a moral rule depends on whether it promotes the greatest happiness, not on tradition alone.

nuance.analogy: Acceptability is a bouncer's guest list: it decides who may enter according to the rules, not just whether you showed up.
nuance.etymology: From acceptable plus -ity, from Latin accipere, to receive.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as acceptibility, with i instead of a in the stem.
Using acceptability as a casual word for acceptance; they mean different things.

senses.definition: The reaction of a substance with acetic acid or one of its derivatives; the introduction of one or more acetyl groups into a substance.
senses.example: Researchers studied acetylation of histone proteins to see how it affected gene expression in the cells.

core.definition: The chemical reaction that adds an acetyl group to a molecule, such as a histone or protein, often changing how it works.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAY, with a lighter stress on SET. The -ation ending is AY-shun, and the middle syllables reduce to uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a precise research term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Mostly used in biochemistry, genetics and pharmacology papers, where scientists speak of histone acetylation, protein acetylation or acetylation status. Americans do not use it outside research. It is often confused with acetylene, the welding gas.

distinctions.note: Adds a methyl group rather than an acetyl group; the two modifications can have different effects on gene activity.
A flammable gas used in welding; the words look alike but name unrelated substances.

examples.everyday: My sister is studying genetics and keeps talking about acetylation, which I still don't fully understand.
examples.professional: Our model tracks acetylation patterns across the promoter regions to predict which genes switch on.
examples.analytical: Histone acetylation generally loosens chromatin, making DNA more accessible to the transcription machinery.

nuance.analogy: Like loosening a tightly wound spool of thread so the thread can be pulled out more easily.
nuance.etymology: From acetylate, from acetyl plus the noun suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Confusing acetylation with acetylene, the welding gas.
Stressing the first syllable instead of LAY.

senses.definition: The state of being acquainted.
A relationship as acquaintances.

core.definition: The state of knowing someone slightly, or a relationship between people who know each other only casually.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KWAYN, and the -ance part reduces to a weak tuhns. Do not pronounce every vowel, and keep the final -ship short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a relationship that is real but not close, often with a slightly formal tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use acquaintanceship in conversation, since they would more often say we know each other or we're acquainted. It appears in formal writing, in obituaries, and in academic or legal descriptions of how well people know each other. In casual speech, say we've met a few times or we're not close.

distinctions.note: Acquaintance usually refers to a single person you know a little, while acquaintanceship refers to the relationship or the state of knowing someone.
Friendship implies warmth and mutual commitment, whereas acquaintanceship implies only casual familiarity.

examples.everyday: Our acquaintanceship started at a church picnic, and now we say hello whenever we pass in the grocery store.
examples.professional: Our acquaintanceship dates from a conference panel, so I know her work but not her team's priorities.
examples.analytical: A bare acquaintanceship differs from friendship because it rests on shared context rather than mutual commitment.

nuance.analogy: An acquaintanceship is like a bridge you cross occasionally without ever building a house on the other side.
nuance.etymology: From acquaintance, from acquaint, plus the suffix -ship denoting a state or relationship.
common_mistakes: Using acquaintanceship when you mean a single person you know slightly; the word for that person is acquaintance.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in uh-kwayn-tuhns-SHIP, which blurs the word.

senses.definition: An abbreviation formed by the initial letters of other words.
senses.example: NASA is an acronym for the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

senses.definition: Generally such abbreviations, including those pronounced as individual letters (initialisms such as "TNT").
senses.example: Many of the terms in our pipeline, such as ETL and API, are acronyms we say letter by letter.

senses.definition: Exclusively such abbreviations when pronounced as a word (as "laser" or "NATO").
An abbreviation formed by the beginning letters or syllables of other words; this sense includes syllabic abbreviations such as Benelux and satnav.
senses.example: The word Benelux is an acronym built from the first syllables of three countries' names.

senses.definition: To form into an acronym.
senses.example: The team decided to acronym the long project name so it would fit on the slide.

core.definition: A word formed from the first letters of a phrase and pronounced as one word, such as NATO or laser.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the last syllable sounds like 'nim', not 'nime' or 'nigh-m'. The r is clearly pronounced and the middle syllable is a weak schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral technical term used in everyday and professional speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often call any abbreviation an acronym, even those pronounced letter by letter like FBI, though strict usage calls those initialisms. In offices and tech work, acronyms are everywhere, and people often ask what one stands for. Saying 'spell out the acronym' is a natural request in meetings.

distinctions.note: An abbreviation is any shortened form, such as Dr. or Jan., while an acronym is formed from initial letters and read as a word.
An initialism is pronounced letter by letter, like FBI, while a true acronym is pronounced as a word, like NASA.

examples.everyday: What does FAQ stand for? It's an acronym for frequently asked questions.
examples.professional: Could you add a glossary of acronyms to the project document so new team members can follow along?
examples.analytical: Strictly speaking, an acronym is pronounced as a word, so FBI is an initialism rather than an acronym.

nuance.analogy: An acronym is like a compressed file that packs a whole phrase into a few initial letters.
nuance.etymology: From Greek akros (tip, extremity) and onoma (name), coined in the early twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Calling every abbreviation an acronym; Dr. and Jan. are abbreviations, not acronyms.
Pronouncing the ending as 'nime' or 'nigh-m' instead of 'nim'.

acronym.etymology: German *Akronym* (from Ancient Greek *ἄκρον* (“end; peak”) + *ὄνυμα* (“name”)), modelled after *Homonym* and *Synonym*, first attested in German in the early 1900s and in English in 1940.

senses.definition: Something to be added; especially text added as an appendix or supplement to a document.
senses.example: An addendum was added to the contract to clarify payment terms.

senses.definition: A postscript.
senses.example: The contract included an addendum that extended the warranty by one year.

senses.definition: The height by which the tooth of a gear projects beyond (outside for external, or inside for internal) the standard pitch circle or pitch line.
senses.example: The gear designer calculated the addendum to ensure smooth meshing with the pinion.

core.definition: Something added to the end of a document, such as an appendix, supplement, or extra note that completes it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, DEN, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'dum' rather than 'doom'. Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the final vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical addition to a document and carries no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use addendum mostly in business, legal, academic, and technical writing, such as a contract addendum or a report addendum. In everyday speech, people usually say 'extra page' or 'update' instead. The plural is addenda, though 'addendums' is also accepted in American business writing.

distinctions.note: An appendix is usually at the back of a book and is part of the original plan, while an addendum is added later to update or correct the document.
A supplement adds material to extend a publication, while an addendum is usually shorter and tied to a specific correction or change.

examples.everyday: Hey, I added a quick addendum to the lease, so check the last page before you sign.
examples.professional: I've attached an addendum to the project proposal that covers the revised budget and timeline.
examples.analytical: The author's addendum modifies the original argument by acknowledging the limitations of the sample.

nuance.analogy: An addendum is like a sticky note added to the bottom of a printed page with a new fact you forgot to include.
nuance.etymology: From Latin addendum, 'something to be added,' the neuter gerundive of addere, 'to add.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AD-en-dum.
Using addendum for a plural set of additions without changing it to addenda.

senses.definition: Lying next to, close, or contiguous; neighboring; bordering on.
senses.example: Because the conference room is filled, we will have our meeting in the adjacent room.

senses.definition: Just before, after, or facing.
senses.example: The picture is on the adjacent page.

senses.definition: Related to; suggestive of; bordering on.
senses.example: The lecture's claims were adjacent to conspiracy theories, which concerned several faculty members.

senses.definition: Something that lies next to something else, especially the side of a right triangle that is neither the hypotenuse nor the opposite.
senses.example: The sine of the angle equals the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse, not the adjacent.

senses.definition: Next to; beside.
senses.example: The house adjacent to the school was demolished.

senses.definition: Related to; suggestive of; bordering on.
senses.example: The lecture's claims were adjacent to conspiracy theories, which concerned several faculty members.

core.definition: Next to or near something, especially sharing a border or side with it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, JAY. The c is pronounced like s, and the final -ent is unstressed, sounding like 'unt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds precise and slightly formal compared with next to.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use adjacent for things that touch or sit close together, such as rooms, buildings or lots, as in 'the room adjacent to the kitchen.' In casual speech they say next to or right next door. In math and science it is the standard term for sides and vertices that touch.

distinctions.note: Next to is casual and everyday, while adjacent is more precise and often used in writing or formal descriptions.
Near means close without necessarily touching, while adjacent usually means touching or sharing a boundary.
Adjoining means touching along a boundary; adjacent can also mean simply close, and it is more common in technical contexts.

examples.everyday: Our hotel room was adjacent to the ice machine, so it was noisy all night.
examples.professional: Please book the conference room adjacent to the kitchen so catering can set up quietly.
examples.analytical: Two ideas are adjacent in this argument when one naturally leads to the next, even if neither is derived from it.

nuance.analogy: Like neighbors who share a fence: close and touching, not just in the same town.
nuance.etymology: From Latin adjacens, lying near, from ad, to, plus jacere, to lie.
common_mistakes: Using adjacent with or instead of to; the usual phrase is adjacent to.
Pronouncing the c as k; it is pronounced like s.

adjacent.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *adiacēns*, *adiacentis*, derivative of *adiaceō* (“to lie beside”); from *ad* (“to”) + *iaceō* (“to lie down”).

senses.definition: One who administers affairs; one who directs, manages, executes, or dispenses, whether in civil, judicial, political, or ecclesiastical affairs; a manager.
senses.example: The administrator of our small hospital meets with department heads every Tuesday morning.

senses.definition: A person who manages or settles the estate of an intestate, or of a testator when there is no competent executor; one to whom the right of administration has been committed by competent authority.
senses.example: The probate court named a local lawyer as administrator of the late widower's estate.

senses.definition: One who is responsible for software installation, management, information and maintenance of a computer or network.
senses.example: As the network administrator, Maria patches servers and maintains backups for the entire company.

core.definition: A person who manages the daily running of an organization, school, hospital, or program, or who manages the affairs of an estate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the MIN syllable and reduce the other syllables to weak vowels. The final -tor is an r-colored schwa, so say 'tur', not 'tor' as in 'door'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role without praise or criticism, although people may use it in a mildly negative way for those who seem focused on rules rather than goals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use administrator for school principals and district leaders, hospital managers, university staff and software or network staff. A 'system administrator' or 'sysadmin' manages computers and networks. In probate courts, an estate administrator handles a deceased person's property.

distinctions.note: A manager leads people and day-to-day work directly, while an administrator is often more focused on rules, records, and running the organization's systems.
An executive is a senior decision-maker who sets strategy, while an administrator usually carries out policy and handles operations.

examples.everyday: The hospital administrator called me back about the billing mix-up.
examples.professional: Our system administrator will reset your password after the security audit.
examples.analytical: A good administrator applies rules impartially, but a leader must also decide which goals those rules are meant to serve.

nuance.analogy: An administrator is like the stage manager of a theater: they keep the schedule, the equipment and the people in the right place so the performance can happen.
nuance.etymology: From Latin administrator, one who manages, from administrare, to manage or serve.
common_mistakes: Confusing administrator with administrative; 'She is an administrative' is wrong, but 'She is an administrator' or 'She works in administration' is correct.
Stressing the final syllable, as in 'ad-min-ih-STRAY-tor'.

senses.definition: Receiving others kindly and conversing with them in a free and friendly manner; friendly, courteous, sociable.
senses.example: Our new neighbor is affable, always waving from his porch and asking about the kids.

senses.definition: Mild; benign.
senses.example: After a week of rain, the affable spring weather finally let us walk the dog outside.

core.definition: Friendly, warm and easy to talk to, putting people at ease in conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and the last two syllables are weak, so the ending sounds like buhl. Do not add an extra syllable such as af-ah-bull.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a warm, approachable person and sounds polished rather than casual.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use affable more in writing, reviews and news than in everyday speech. In conversation they might say nice or easy to talk to instead. Calling a host, doctor or coworker affable is a compliment that signals warmth with some polish.

distinctions.note: Friendly is the everyday word for warmth; affable suggests a relaxed, sociable manner that puts others at ease.
Amiable focuses on a pleasant, good-natured disposition; affable adds the idea of being easy to talk to.

examples.everyday: The guy at the hardware store was really affable and walked me straight to the right aisle.
examples.professional: Our new account manager is affable on calls, so clients tend to stay longer and share more about their needs.
examples.analytical: A good interlocutor is affable without being servile, giving others room to speak while keeping the argument honest.

nuance.analogy: An affable person is like a comfortable sofa: approachable and easy to settle into.
nuance.etymology: From Latin affabilis, easy to address, from affari, to speak to.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in af-AH-bul.
Using affable for someone who was nice for a single moment; it describes a steady, pleasant manner.

affable.etymology: French *affable*, from Latin *affābilis*, from *affor* (“to address”), from *ad* + *for* (“to speak, to talk”).

senses.definition: The part of the day from noon or lunchtime until sunset, evening, or suppertime or 6pm.
senses.example: I spent yesterday afternoon at the memorial service for grandpa.

senses.definition: The later part of anything, often with implications of decline.
senses.example: In the afternoon of his career, he began mentoring young players instead of chasing titles.

senses.definition: A party or social event held in the afternoon.
senses.example: We're hosting an afternoon for the neighbors on Saturday, with lemonade, cake, and lawn games.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of good afternoon.

core.definition: The part of the day between noon and evening, roughly from lunchtime until about five or six o'clock or sunset.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, NOON, with a lighter secondary stress on AF. Many learners say AF-ter-noon with equal stress, but Americans reduce the middle syllable to a quick r-colored schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a time of day with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'good afternoon' as a greeting from around noon until early evening, then switch to 'good evening' once it gets dark. People say 'this afternoon' for later today and 'yesterday afternoon' for earlier. A natural reply to 'Good afternoon' is 'Good afternoon, how are you?' or simply 'Hi'.

distinctions.note: Evening begins around sunset and runs until bedtime, while afternoon ends when evening starts; people switch greetings at dusk.
Noon is the single moment of midday, while afternoon is the whole period after it.
Midday is a more general word for the middle of the day, often used in news or weather forecasts; afternoon refers to the time after lunch.

examples.everyday: Let's grab lunch this afternoon, maybe around one o'clock?
examples.professional: The client review has been moved to Thursday afternoon, so please update your calendars.
examples.analytical: Historians sometimes describe the late Roman period as the afternoon of the empire, when decline was already visible.

nuance.analogy: The afternoon is like the downhill part of a hike: the summit has passed, and the trail slopes toward the evening.
nuance.etymology: Compound of after and noon, from Middle English aftern and noon.
common_mistakes: Using 'in' with a specific day, as in 'in Monday afternoon'; Americans say 'on Monday afternoon'.
Writing 'after noon' as two words when meaning the time of day; the usual form is one word.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to, the ownership, tenure and cultivation of land.
Agricultural or rural.
Wild; said of plants growing in a cultivated field.
senses.example: Wild agrarian oats sprouted between the rows of wheat, and the farmer pulled them by hand.

senses.definition: A person who advocates the political interests of working farmers.
senses.example: As a longtime agrarian, my uncle fought for price supports that protected family farms.

core.definition: Relating to farming, farmland, or land ownership, especially in a rural society where farming is the main economic activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, GRAIR, which sounds like 'air' with an r. The final syllable is a reduced 'ee-un,' so do not say 'ah-GRAIR-ee-an' with an open a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an economic or social system without clear praise or criticism, though it can carry political meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use agrarian mainly in history, economics, and political discussions about rural life or land policy. In everyday talk, 'farm' or 'rural' is more natural. For farming activity itself, 'agricultural' is the usual word, while agrarian often refers to a whole way of life or a political ideal. A natural reply is to ask about the time period or the policy being discussed.

distinctions.note: Agricultural describes farming activities and methods, while agrarian describes a society, economy, or political ideal centered on land and farming.
Rural means related to the countryside in general, while agrarian focuses on land cultivation and farmers as an economic or political class.

examples.everyday: My grandparents grew up in an agrarian town where almost everyone grew something in their backyard.
examples.professional: The policy team is reviewing how drought insurance affects small farms in our agrarian regions.
examples.analytical: Jefferson's vision of a republic of independent farmers rested on an agrarian ideal in which land ownership supported civic virtue.

nuance.analogy: Like a town built around its river, with its whole economy and identity shaped by the land beneath it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin agrarius, 'of fields,' from ager, 'field.'
common_mistakes: Using agrarian for any farming activity, when agricultural is the usual word for farming methods.
Pronouncing it with a full open vowel, as in 'ah-GRAIR-ee-an,' instead of the reduced final syllable.

agrarian.etymology: From Middle French *agrarien*, from Latin *agrarius* (“of the land”), from stem of *ager* (“field”) + *-arius*.

senses.definition: To harmonize in opinion, statement, or action; to be in unison or concord; to be or become united or consistent; to concur.
senses.example: all parties agree in the expediency of the law.

senses.definition: To yield assent; to accede;—followed by to.
senses.example: to agree to an offer, or to opinion.

senses.definition: To make a stipulation by way of settling differences or determining a price; to exchange promises; to come to terms or to a common resolve; to promise.
senses.example: The two companies agreed to split the cost of the pipeline and sign the contract next month.

senses.definition: To be conformable; to resemble; to coincide; to correspond.
senses.example: the picture does not agree with the original; the two scales agree exactly.

senses.definition: (now always with with) To suit or be adapted in its effects; to do well.
senses.example: the same food does not agree with every constitution.

senses.definition: (grammar) To correspond to (another word) in a grammatical category, such as gender, number, case, or person.
senses.example: In Romanian, the articles, adjectives, pronouns agree in gender, number and case with the noun they refer to.

senses.definition: To consent to a contract or to an element of a contract.
senses.example: The tenants agreed to the new lease terms, including the higher rent and the shorter notice period.

core.definition: To have the same opinion as someone, or to say yes to a plan, request or arrangement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable 'GREE' with a long e, and keep the first syllable a weak schwa. Don't say 'AG-ree' with the stress on the first syllable, and remember that 'agreed' is pronounced 'uh-GREED'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It signals cooperation and shared understanding, and 'I agree' is a warm, natural reply.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'I agree' in everyday conversation, and 'Agreed!' is a common casual reply to a suggestion. Use 'agree with' for opinions and people, 'agree to' for accepting a plan or terms, and 'agree on' for a choice such as a time or place. In a meeting, 'I agree' followed by a reason sounds more professional than a bare yes.

distinctions.note: Consent is a more formal word for giving permission, often in legal or medical contexts, while agree is the everyday word for sharing an opinion or accepting a plan.
Concur is a formal word used in professional or legal writing, while agree is the ordinary word Americans use in conversation and email.
Accept means to receive or take something, such as an offer or a gift, while agree means to share an opinion or consent to terms.

examples.everyday: We agreed on pizza for dinner, so I'll place the order now.
examples.professional: I agree with your point about the timeline, but we still need legal to approve the scope before we commit.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers agree that moral claims require reasons, though they disagree about what counts as a good reason.

nuance.analogy: Like two people walking the same path, agreement means you end up going in the same direction.
nuance.etymology: From Old French agreer, 'to please or accept', from a- 'to' and gre 'liking or will'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I agree you' instead of 'I agree with you'.
Using 'agree the plan' instead of 'agree to the plan' or 'agree on the plan'.

agree.etymology: From Middle English *agreen*, from Old French *agreer* (“to accept or receive kindly”), from *a gré* (“favorably”), from Latin *ad* (“to”) + *gratus* (“pleasing”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **gʷerH-* (“to welcome, greet, praise”).

senses.definition: A doctrine of non-violence, concerned with the sacredness of all living things and an effort to avoid causing harm to them.
senses.example: Gandhi's commitment to ahimsa shaped his approach to protest and civil disobedience.

core.definition: In Hinduism, Jainism and Buddhism, the principle of non-violence toward all living beings, including avoiding harm in thought, speech and action.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, HIM. The first syllable is a light, reduced vowel, and the h is breathy, so avoid pronouncing it as a hard AH-hims-uh.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful; it signals moral seriousness and spiritual discipline, and can sound preachy if used in a casual argument about food or chores.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ahimsa mainly when discussing Indian religions, yoga, vegetarianism, or Gandhi's and Martin Luther King Jr.'s approach to nonviolent resistance. It is a formal, respectful term rather than slang, so it is best used in discussions of ethics or religion. In everyday talk, 'nonviolence' is the more common choice.

distinctions.note: Nonviolence is the general English term for refusing to use force; ahimsa is a specific spiritual principle that extends to all living things.
Pacifism is a political or moral position against war and military force, while ahimsa is a broader principle that covers daily conduct and even thought.

examples.everyday: My roommate is vegan because she follows ahimsa, and she won't even use leather shoes.
examples.professional: Our community nonprofit uses an ahimsa-based approach, so we never use coercion to win local support.
examples.analytical: Gandhi's ahimsa was not passive submission; it required active courage in refusing to return violence with violence.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who avoids stepping on any seedling, ahimsa asks you to watch where your actions land on every living thing.
nuance.etymology: From Sanskrit ahiṃsā, 'non-injury', from a- 'not' plus hiṃsā 'injury'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (AH-him-suh) instead of the second.
Assuming ahimsa only means avoiding violence against people, when it covers animals and all life.

senses.definition: (rare) Streamlined.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Shaped or streamlined so that air flows past it with little resistance, such as a car body or aircraft nose.

pronunciation.tip: In a compound adjective before a noun, Americans usually stress the first word, so AIR gets the main stress. The final -ed is a clear /d/ after the voiced th, so say 'smoothd' as one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests sleek, efficient, or graceful design.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word, found mainly in design writing, technical descriptions, or literary praise of machines. Americans normally say 'streamlined' or 'aerodynamic' in everyday and technical talk. You will rarely need it in conversation, but it helps when reading older or literary texts.

distinctions.note: Streamlined is the common everyday term for a sleek shape, while air-smoothed is rarer and emphasizes that the air has been smoothed around the object.
Aerodynamic is the precise technical term for shapes that reduce air resistance, while air-smoothed is a more descriptive and literary choice.

examples.everyday: Those old racing cars have that air-smoothed look, like they were carved for speed.
examples.professional: The prototype's air-smoothed nose reduced drag by a noticeable amount in the wind tunnel tests.
examples.analytical: The poet praised the air-smoothed curves of the aircraft as if they were the graceful lines of a bird in flight.

nuance.analogy: Like a river stone worn smooth, but shaped by moving air instead of water.
nuance.etymology: Compound of air and smoothed, the past participle of smooth (from Old English smoþ).
common_mistakes: Saying 'smoo-thed' as two syllables instead of one.
Using it in everyday talk where streamlined or aerodynamic is more natural.

senses.definition: Cold, chilly; used of low body temperature, especially in connection with certain diseases such as malaria and cholera.
senses.example: algid malaria

core.definition: Very cold, chilly, especially describing a low body temperature during illness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the 'g' as a 'j' sound, like 'jump'. The final 'id' is short, rhyming with 'rid' or 'kid'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and clinical. It describes an unpleasant cold, often in a medical context, and it sounds formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use 'algid' in conversation; it belongs to medical history and older literary writing. A doctor might describe a patient as algid in a historical or pathology context. In everyday talk, say 'chilled' or 'freezing'.

distinctions.note: Chilly is ordinary and mild; algid is formal and suggests a clinically dangerous low temperature.
Frigid can describe weather or a cold personality; algid is limited to physical cold, often of the body.

examples.professional: The clinical report described the patient as algid, which told the team the infection had reached a critical stage.
examples.analytical: Historical accounts of cholera describe the algid phase, in which the body loses heat and the skin turns clammy and blue.

nuance.analogy: If a fever is a furnace running too hot, algid is the furnace gone cold, with the body losing heat it cannot replace.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'algidus', meaning 'cold', from 'algere', 'to be cold'.
common_mistakes: Using 'algid' for ordinary cold weather; it is too clinical for everyday use.
Confusing it with 'acid' because of the similar spelling; the words are unrelated.

senses.definition: To convert an informal description of a process or a procedure into an algorithm.

core.definition: To turn an informal description of a process into a precise, step-by-step algorithm that a computer can run.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress stays on AL, not on the -ize ending, even though the verb is built from 'algorithm'. Pronounce the final syllable as 'mize', rhyming with 'eyes'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a technical task and carries no praise or criticism by itself.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized verb used mostly in computer science, mathematics, and technical writing. Americans would more often say 'write an algorithm for' or 'formalize the rules' in everyday work. Use it when you want to emphasize converting a vague human process into exact computational steps.

distinctions.note: To formalize is to state something in rigorous logical or mathematical terms, while to algorithmize specifically means producing a step-by-step procedure for a machine.
To automate means to make a process run without human effort, while algorithmizing is the design step that makes automation possible.

examples.everyday: Grandma's recipe says 'add flour until it feels right,' so I'm trying to algorithmize it into exact measurements.
examples.professional: We need to algorithmize the approval rules before the engineers can automate them.
examples.analytical: Turning moral judgment into a fixed rule set risks algorithmizing ambiguity, leaving no room for the context that wise judgment requires.

nuance.analogy: Algorithmizing is like turning a grandmother's handwritten recipe into a numbered list that anyone can follow exactly.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from 'algorithm' with the verb-forming suffix '-ize'.
common_mistakes: Using it for general coding, when the word specifically means converting a described process into a precise procedure.
Putting the stress on the final syllable instead of AL.

senses.definition: Making no significant difference.
senses.example: It's all the same to me if you want to leave early.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see all,‎ same.
senses.example: His speeches are all the same.

senses.definition: Anyway; nevertheless; nonetheless.
senses.example: He knew it was risky. He did it all the same.

core.definition: Nevertheless; even so, in spite of what was just said or done. Often accepts something while still making a point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAME, which has the diphthong in 'name', not 'sahm'. 'The' reduces to 'thuh' before a consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes resigned or gracious. Tone decides whether it sounds polite or a little dismissive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'all the same' to accept something while still holding a view or to thank someone politely, for example 'I know it's late, but thanks for coming all the same.' It is conversational. In formal writing, 'nevertheless' or 'nonetheless' fits better. Adding 'thanks' often makes it sound warmer.

distinctions.note: 'Anyway' is casual and can change the subject, while 'all the same' keeps the topic and shows reluctant acceptance.
'Nevertheless' is formal and written, while 'all the same' is conversational.

collocations: it's all the same to me
it would be nice all the same

examples.everyday: I know you're busy, but thanks for the invite all the same.
examples.professional: The budget is tight and the timeline is aggressive; all the same, we'll aim to finish the migration by Friday.
examples.analytical: Critics note the small sample, but the findings all the same point to a pattern worth testing in larger populations.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who knows the road is icy but still drives carefully toward the destination.
nuance.etymology: From the idiom 'all the same', meaning 'it comes to the same thing', which developed into the sense 'nevertheless'.
common_mistakes: Reading it as 'identical' in a comparison; 'all the same' usually means 'nevertheless' in speech.
Using 'all the same' in formal writing where 'nevertheless' or 'nonetheless' fits better.

senses.definition: To reduce or lessen the severity of a pain or difficulty.
senses.example: alleviate his pain

senses.definition: To pay down partially.
senses.example: There are different ways to alleviate your financial debt.

core.definition: To make pain, suffering or a problem less severe or easier to bear, though not always to remove it completely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LEE. The middle vowels are reduced to ih and uh, and the final -ate is ayt, not it.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying relief or improvement; it appears in medical, political and everyday contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alleviate in formal writing, medical settings and news, as in the medication alleviates pain. In casual speech they say ease, help with or make it better, so alleviate sounds a little formal. In a meeting you might say This should help alleviate some of the pressure. A natural reply is Thanks, that really helps.

distinctions.note: Relieve is more common and everyday; alleviate is more formal and often refers to lessening a condition.
Cure means to end an illness completely; alleviate only makes it less severe.
Ease is informal and gentle; alleviate is precise and formal.

examples.everyday: Try some honey tea; it might help alleviate that scratchy throat.
examples.professional: Adding a second on-call engineer should alleviate the pressure on the incident rotation.
examples.analytical: Theodicy asks whether suffering can be alleviated by God's presence without being explained away.

nuance.analogy: Like loosening a tight knot: the knot remains, but it no longer pinches.
nuance.etymology: From Latin alleviare 'to lighten', from ad 'to' and levis 'light'.
common_mistakes: Using alleviate to mean completely remove; it means make less severe
Stressing the last syllable as uh-lee-VAYT

alleviate.etymology: Late Latin *alleviatus*, past participle of *allevio* (“to lighten; to alleviate”).

senses.definition: Encouraging or calling attention to a physical performance, especially one involving an upwards lift or leap.
senses.example: Alley oop! shouted Dad as he hoisted his daughter onto his shoulders.

senses.definition: Synonym of up.
senses.example: He swung the toddler alley oop onto the top of the wall.

senses.definition: An instance of saying "Alley oop!"
senses.example: Dad's cheerful alley oop before each lift made the kids giggle every time.

senses.definition: A high and arcing pass, catch, or move, especially a shot made by a player as part of the same jump used to catch a pass.
senses.example: The guard threw a perfect alley oop to the center, who dunked it.

senses.definition: Involving at least a 180-degree turn.
senses.example: The skater landed an alley oop spin, turning completely around before touching the ice.

senses.definition: High and arcing.
senses.example: He lofted an alley oop shot that floated over the defender's outstretched hand.

senses.definition: To lift or toss upward, or to be lifted or tossed upward.
senses.example: The point guard alley oops the ball to the forward every time the defense collapses.

core.definition: An informal cry, or a play, in which a player leaps to catch a high pass thrown toward the basket or goal, often for a dunk or slam.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, 'up', and the first two syllables are quick and light. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce it as 'alley-OOP' with a long a, when it is closer to 'al-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and playful. It signals excitement or teamwork and is used for both real lifts and joking encouragement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Alley-oop!' most often in basketball, cheerleading, gymnastics, and playground settings, and sometimes to tease someone who is helped up. The spelling 'alley-oop' with a hyphen is standard in American writing. A natural reply is a cheer, a laugh, or just a 'Nice!'

distinctions.note: A lob is any high, arcing shot or pass in sports such as tennis or volleyball, while an alley-oop specifically involves a teammate catching the ball in the air and finishing with a jump.
A dunk is the act of pushing the ball down through the hoop, which can be done in many ways; an alley-oop is a particular kind of dunk, set up by a pass.

examples.everyday: When my son reached for the monkey bars, his dad lifted him up and yelled, Alley-oop!
examples.professional: For the company softball game, Dan wants to run an alley-oop from the shortstop to the first baseman as a surprise play.
examples.analytical: The alley-oop is a useful case study in coordinated motion, since the pass must arrive exactly where the jumper will be rising.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay in which the second runner is already moving when the baton arrives, the alley-oop depends on timing that happens in midair.
nuance.etymology: Of uncertain origin; it is thought to come from French 'allez hop' or 'allez-oop', a cry to encourage a lift.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'AL-ley-oop', instead of the last syllable.
Writing it as one word or as 'ali-oop' in formal writing; the standard form is 'alley-oop'.

alley-oop.etymology: Borrowed from French *allez-hop*, the cry of a circus acrobat about to leap.

senses.definition: The property of being alterable.
senses.example: The engineers tested the alterability of the polymer under extreme temperatures.

core.definition: The quality of being capable of being changed or modified.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress shifts to BIL, in the syllable before '-ability', so it is not ALter-ability. The 'a' in the middle is a reduced schwa, and the ending is 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise word used in analysis and policy, not everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use alterability mainly in science, law, philosophy and policy writing when discussing whether something can be changed. In everyday talk they usually say changeability or 'how easy it is to change.' The word sounds stiff in a casual setting, so use it in formal or analytical writing.

distinctions.note: Changeability is the everyday word for how easily something changes, while alterability is more formal and specific to what can be altered.
Mutability is formal and often describes change over time in nature or character, while alterability emphasizes that something is capable of being modified.

examples.everyday: The shirt fits fine, but I'm not sure about the alterability of the sleeves.
examples.professional: We should test the alterability of the model's parameters before we deploy it to production.
examples.analytical: Philosophers debate whether the alterability of human nature supports or undermines moral responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like clay: its alterability is what makes it useful for shaping.
nuance.etymology: From alterable, from alter, from Late Latin alterare, 'to make other'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as ALter-ability; the main stress is on BIL.
Using alterability in casual speech, where changeability is more natural.

senses.definition: The juice from chewing tobacco.

core.definition: The brown liquid released when someone chews tobacco and spits it out.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced, rhotic 'er', like the end of 'water'. Don't pronounce it 'am-BEER'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and crude. It describes something unpleasant and is considered dated.
nuance.usage_note: This word is archaic and mainly appears in older American fiction or in dialect writing about rural life. Today people say 'tobacco juice' or 'chew spit' in ordinary speech. It is not suitable for polite conversation, and most listeners would not recognize it.

distinctions.note: The chew is the plug of tobacco itself, while ambeer is the liquid it releases.

examples.professional: Workplace safety training covers the hygiene and health risks of spitting tobacco juice.
examples.analytical: The novel's references to ambeer mark its rural characters as coarse and outside polite society.

nuance.analogy: Like an old-fashioned word for a brown stain, one that people no longer use but still find in old books.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'amber', the golden-brown color or fossil resin.
Pronouncing it 'am-BEER' with the stress on the second syllable.

ambeer.etymology: Alteration of *amber*, due to its colour.

senses.definition: A view in Christian eschatology that rejects the claimed future thousand-year physical reign of Jesus Christ on the earth, in opposition to premillennial and some postmillennial views of the Book of Revelation, chapter 20, claiming instead that the number of years in Revelation 20 is a symbolic number and that Christ's eventual physical reign will be permanent.
senses.example: Our study group debated amillennialism, comparing its symbolic reading of Revelation 20 with premillennial interpretations.

core.definition: The view that the thousand years of Revelation 20 are symbolic, not a future earthly reign, and that Christ's reign is now.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LEN, with secondary stress on 'ay.' The prefix a- is pronounced 'ay,' like the letter A, and not 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is a label for a position, and the name can mislead since it does not deny the Millennium entirely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in theology, especially among Reformed, Lutheran, and Catholic scholars. The 'a-' prefix means 'no,' but amillennialists do accept a millennium, interpreted spiritually. It is often explained in contrast with premillennialism and postmillennialism.

distinctions.note: 'Premillennialism' expects a literal thousand-year reign after Christ returns, but amillennialism reads the thousand years as symbolic of the present age.
'Postmillennialism' expects a coming golden age before Christ returns, whereas amillennialism does not expect such an era.
'Realized millennialism' is another name for amillennialism, stressing that the Millennium is already present in the Church.

examples.everyday: I grew up Lutheran, so I guess I was taught amillennialism without ever hearing the word.
examples.professional: The commentary explains why many Reformed scholars favor amillennialism in reading Revelation 20.
examples.analytical: Amillennialism treats the thousand years as a symbol of the present age between Christ's resurrection and his return, so Christ reigns now.

nuance.analogy: The thousand years are like a symbol for the whole church age, not a separate calendar chapter.
nuance.etymology: From Greek a-, 'not, without' + Latin millennium + -ism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the a- as 'uh' instead of 'ay.'
Thinking it denies any Millennium at all.
Stressing the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Amillennialists read Revelation 20:1-6 as symbolic, seeing the binding of Satan as the effect of Christ's first coming, as in Matthew 12:29, where Jesus speaks of binding the strong man. They also read the first resurrection as spiritual life with Christ, and note that John 5:28-29 speaks of one general resurrection at the last hour.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology is generally close to an amillennial reading, seeing Christ's reign as present in the Church, though it does not use that label as a formal doctrine.
Catholic teaching, following Augustine, traditionally treats the thousand years symbolically as the age of the Church, and is commonly described as amillennial in effect.

Amillennialism is held by Lutherans, many Reformed Christians, and many Anglicans, who follow Augustine in reading the thousand years as symbolic. Many Baptists and Pentecostals instead hold premillennial views.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to amillennialism.
senses.example: The amillennialist commentary argued that the thousand years represent the present church age.

senses.definition: A believer in amillennialism.
senses.example: As an amillennialist, our pastor teaches that Christ already reigns through his church.

core.definition: A Christian who reads the thousand-year reign in Revelation 20 as a symbol of the present church age, not a future earthly kingdom.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEN, the third syllable, as in millennial. The word has an 'ee-uh' sound in the middle and ends in 'list', not 'lyst' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a theological position and is used in classrooms and church debates, sometimes with strong feelings on both sides.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in seminary courses, theology books, church discussions about end times, and Bible study. Many believers don't use the word at all, so you might hear 'I believe the thousand years is symbolic'. Use the adjective 'amillennial' for views and the noun 'amillennialist' for a person who holds them.

distinctions.note: A premillennialist believes Christ will return before a literal thousand-year earthly reign, while an amillennialist reads that reign as symbolic of the present church age.
A postmillennialist expects the church to bring about a golden age before Christ returns, while an amillennialist does not expect a special earthly age before the Second Coming.

examples.everyday: At coffee after Bible study, my friend said she was an amillennialist, so I had to ask her what that meant.
examples.professional: In our seminar syllabus, the amillennialist position is presented alongside the premillennial and postmillennial views.
examples.analytical: An amillennialist reads the thousand years of Revelation 20 as a symbol of Christ's present reign through the church rather than a future interval on earth.

nuance.analogy: Like reading a map of a city with a symbolic scale: the thousand years are not measured in calendar time but represent a complete and perfect period.
nuance.etymology: From Latin a- 'not' and millennium 'thousand years', from mille 'thousand' and annus 'year'.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it with one n or one l, as 'amilennialist'.
Confusing amillennialism with premillennialism because both words describe the timing of Christ's return and the thousand years.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word chilia, meaning 'thousand', is the basis of the term millennium. The thousand years appear in Revelation 20, which is the only passage that describes them. Revelation 20:1-3 describes Satan being bound for a thousand years, and Revelation 20:4-6 describes the faithful reigning with Christ for that period. Amillennialists read these verses symbolically, as describing Christ's present reign through the church, while premillennialists read them as a future earthly kingdom.

traditions.view: Eastern Orthodox Christians generally do not teach a literal earthly millennium of Christ's reign. They read Revelation's imagery in relation to the church's present life and the age to come.

The Roman Catholic Church has not defined a literal millennium. Most Catholic theologians read Revelation 20 symbolically, following Augustine, and the Catechism does not teach a future earthly reign.

Protestants differ. Reformed and Lutheran traditions are largely amillennial, while many Baptist, Pentecostal and dispensational Christians hold premillennial views. Postmillennialism was popular in the nineteenth century.

senses.definition: The measure of the size of something, especially its width or breadth; largeness, magnitude.
The maximum absolute value of the vertical component of a curve or function, especially one that is periodic.
The horizontal line which measures the distance to which a projectile is thrown; the range.
The range of motion of the gymnast's body while performing a skill.
The range of environmental conditions in which an organism can survive.
The maximum absolute value of some quantity that varies.

The arc of the horizon between the true east or west point and the center of the sun, or a star, at its rising or setting. At the rising, the amplitude is eastern or ortive: at the setting, it is western, occiduous, or occasive. It is also northern or southern, when north or south of the equator.
The arc of the horizon between the true east or west point and the foot of the vertical circle passing through any star or object.

core.definition: In mathematics and physics, the maximum displacement of a periodic wave or oscillation from its resting or average value.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on the final syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, and the ending is 'tood' in General American, not the 'tyood' of British speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a technical measurement term with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use amplitude in science, engineering, music and math classes, and in discussions of sound volume or earthquakes. In everyday speech they say 'volume,' 'loudness' or 'size of the wave' instead. The general sense of 'breadth' or 'largeness' is old-fashioned and rarely heard in the US today.

distinctions.note: Amplitude is how big each wave swing is. Frequency is how often the wave repeats per second, so the two are independent.
Magnitude is a general measure of size or strength. Amplitude refers specifically to the maximum displacement of an oscillation or wave.
Altitude is height above sea level. The two words look similar but have completely different meanings.

examples.everyday: When you turn the volume knob up, you're making the amplitude of the sound wave bigger, so it sounds louder.
examples.professional: The sensor's noise floor hides small amplitude changes, so we need to filter the signal before we model the vibration.
examples.analytical: Reducing the amplitude of a pendulum's swing does not change its period, which is why its frequency stays constant even as it slows.

nuance.analogy: Like how far a child's swing goes up and down from the middle: that distance is the amplitude.
nuance.etymology: From Latin amplitudo, 'largeness, breadth,' from amplus 'large.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'altitude,' which is height above sea level.
Saying 'AM-plih-TYOOD,' the British-style ending, instead of the American 'tood.'
Using it in everyday speech where 'volume' or 'loudness' is more natural.

amplitude.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *amplitude*, from Latin *amplitūdō*, from *amplus* (“large”).

senses.definition: That restores or stimulates health.
Of or relating to analepsis (a form of flashback).
senses.example: The film's analeptic structure reveals the murder in the second scene, before we see what led to it.

senses.definition: A restorative or stimulative medication, especially one used to overcome depression.
senses.example: The nurse gave the exhausted patient an analeptic to stimulate her breathing after surgery.

core.definition: Restoring or stimulating health, strength or alertness, especially said of a medicine or drug that revives a patient.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LEP, the third syllable, and the first two syllables are quick and light. The -ic ending is short, like 'tick', not 'tee-k'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a medical effect and carries no emotional judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, pharmacologists and medical writers use this word to describe a stimulant that restores breathing or alertness. Most Americans would say 'stimulant' or 'pick-me-up' instead, and in a literature class you might hear the separate sense of 'analepsis', a flashback. As a noun, it names the drug itself and is most common in medical texts.

distinctions.note: Restorative is a general word for anything that revives health, while analeptic is narrower and specifically names a stimulant drug.
Stimulant is the everyday American word for anything that increases alertness, while analeptic is a technical word used in medicine.

examples.everyday: The doctor said I didn't need an analeptic for the fatigue, I just needed more sleep and fewer late nights.
examples.professional: The pharmacology team reviewed which analeptic agents remain approved for treating respiratory depression in hospital patients.
examples.analytical: Pharmacologists debate whether an analeptic should be classified as a true stimulant or as a restorative that merely supports the body's own recovery.

nuance.analogy: Like jump-starting a car battery: the drug gives the system a jolt so it can run on its own again.
nuance.etymology: From Greek analēptikos ('restoring'), from analambanein ('to take up again').
common_mistakes: Confusing analeptic, a stimulant drug, with analepsis, a literary flashback.
Using analeptic in everyday speech where stimulant or pick-me-up is more natural.

senses.definition: That follows necessarily by definition; tautologous.
senses.example: The statement 'all bachelors are unmarried' is analytic, so it cannot be false.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to algebra or a similar method of analysis.
senses.example: She studied analytic geometry, which uses algebraic equations to describe curves.

senses.definition: Being defined in terms of objects of differential calculus such as derivatives.
senses.example: The team's model is analytic, since every term is built from derivatives of the input.

senses.definition: Being able to be locally represented by convergent power series around every point of the domain.
senses.example: A function that is analytic at every point can be written as a convergent power series.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to any form of analysis, or to analytics.
senses.example: analytic method

senses.definition: Of, or relating to division into elements or principles.
senses.example: The philosopher offered an analytic account that breaks the concept into its essential principles.

senses.definition: Having the ability to analyze.
senses.example: Her analytic mind made her the best person to untangle the budget problem.

senses.definition: Of a language, having a grammar principally dependent on the arrangement of uninflected function words within sentences to indicate meaning.
senses.example: Vietnamese is often called analytic because it relies on word order and particles rather than inflections.

senses.definition: A proposed role for each of a society's components.
senses.example: It is tempting to take the case of Islamic traditions as instances of such a counterpublic and generalize this into an analytic of Islamic traditions and modernity tout court. ~Brian Silverstein, Islam and Modernity in Turkey (2010), Palgrave Macmillan, ISBN 978-0-230-10982-7, p. 2.

core.definition: Relying on logical analysis; in philosophy, true by the meaning of its words alone, without checking the world.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, LIT, with a light secondary stress on AN. The middle syllables are reduced to uh and a short i, not 'uh-NAL-ih-tik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use. Describing a person as analytic is mildly positive, suggesting careful, logical thinking.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say 'analytical' for a person who breaks problems down carefully, as in 'She's very analytical'. 'Analytic' is more typical in technical or academic contexts, such as 'analytic philosophy', 'analytic function' or 'analytic geometry'. In a meeting, you can use either, but 'analytical' is the safer everyday choice.

distinctions.note: Analytic is more technical and appears in set phrases like 'analytic philosophy', while analytical is the everyday word for a person's careful thinking style.
In philosophy, an analytic statement is true by definition, while a synthetic statement depends on facts about the world.
Logical is broader and describes any sound reasoning, while analytic is specific to truth that follows from definitions or to breaking things into parts.

examples.everyday: My philosophy professor says 'all bachelors are unmarried' is analytic, so you don't need to check the world to know it's true.
examples.professional: Let's take an analytic approach to the churn problem and break it into measurable drivers before we pick a model.
examples.analytical: Kant's distinction between analytic and synthetic judgments asks whether the predicate is already contained in the concept of the subject.

nuance.analogy: An analytic truth is like a dictionary definition that cannot be wrong, because its truth comes from the words themselves.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'analytikos', 'able to resolve', from 'analyein', 'to unloose or resolve'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'She is analytic' for a person's thinking style. Americans normally say 'She is analytical'.
Putting the stress on the wrong syllable, as in 'uh-NAL-ih-tik'. The stress falls on LIT.

senses.definition: A cone-shaped structure built from sediment and other available materials by ants or white ants (termites), and beneath which the colony nests.
senses.example: A column of soil rose beside the trail, the anthill built by a colony of harvester ants.

core.definition: A mound of soil, sand, or other material built up over the underground nest of an ant colony.

pronunciation.tip: This is a compound, so the main stress falls on the first word, ANT. Say the t clearly before the h, and end with a clear l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a natural structure, but figuratively it can suggest a busy, crowded place full of people moving constantly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use anthill in ordinary speech about ants in a yard or park. You might warn someone, 'Don't stand on that anthill,' or describe a place as 'an anthill' when it is busy. Termite structures are usually called termite mounds, not anthills, even though termites are not ants.

distinctions.note: Mound is a general word for any raised heap of earth, while anthill refers specifically to a structure built by ants.
A termite mound is built by termites, which are not ants, so Americans use termite mound for those structures.

examples.everyday: Be careful where you sit, because there is an anthill right by the picnic table.
examples.professional: The office was an anthill of activity the week before the product launch.
examples.analytical: Entomologists often estimate colony size by counting the entrances on each anthill.

nuance.analogy: Like a city seen from above, where a crowd of busy workers keeps the whole structure running.
nuance.etymology: Compound of ant (Old English æmete) and hill (Old English hyll).
common_mistakes: Calling a termite mound an anthill; termites are not ants, so Americans say termite mound.
Writing ant hill as two words in formal writing, when anthill is the standard spelling.

anthill.etymology: From Middle English *ametehul*, *amptehille*, from Old English *ǣmethyll*, equivalent to *ant* + *hill*.

senses.definition: An application to a superior court or judge for a decision or order by an inferior court or judge to be reviewed and overturned.
senses.example: The losing company filed an appeal asking the higher court to overturn the lower court's ruling.

senses.definition: The legal document or form by which such an application is made; also, the court case in which the application is argued.
senses.example: Her lawyer filed the appeal form with the clerk before the deadline expired on Friday.

senses.definition: A person's legal right to apply to court for such a review.
senses.example: I have an appeal against the lower court decision.

senses.definition: A call to a person or an authority for a decision, help, or proof; an entreaty, an invocation.
senses.example: He made an appeal for volunteers to help at the festival.

senses.definition: A resort to some physical means; a recourse.
senses.example: Having run out of options, he made an appeal to force and kicked the locked door open.

senses.definition: A power to attract or interest.
A use of a principle or quality for purposes of persuasion.
senses.example: The ad's appeal to nostalgia convinced many shoppers to buy the retro-styled sneakers.

senses.definition: The act, by the fielding side, of asking an umpire for a decision on whether a batsman is out or not.
senses.example: The fielders gathered around the bowler and made an appeal, shouting 'Howzat!' at the umpire.

senses.definition: (historical) An accusation or charge against someone for wrongdoing (especially treason).
senses.example: The nobleman's enemies brought an appeal of treason against him, accusing him of plotting to kill the king.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A process which formerly might be instituted by one private person against another for some heinous crime demanding punishment for the particular injury suffered, rather than for the offense against the public; an accusation.
senses.example: In medieval courts, a widow could bring an appeal of murder against the man who had killed her husband.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) At common law, an accusation made against a felon by one of their accomplices (called an approver).
senses.example: The thief's former partner, hoping for leniency, brought an appeal against him at common law.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A summons to defend one's honor in a duel, or one's innocence in a trial by combat; a challenge.
senses.example: Insulted by the remark, the knight sent his rival a formal appeal, demanding a duel at dawn.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Often followed by against (the inferior court's decision) or to (the superior court): to apply to a superior court or judge for a decision or order by an inferior court or judge to be reviewed and overturned.
senses.example: Dissatisfied with the judge’s ruling, she decided to appeal.

senses.definition: To apply to a superior court or judge to review and overturn (a decision or order by an inferior court or judge).
senses.example: The plaintiff appealed the decision to the appellate court.

senses.definition: To call upon a person or an authority to corroborate a statement, to decide a controverted question, or to vindicate one's rights; to entreat, to invoke.
senses.example: Before ruling, the judge will appeal to the constitution to settle the disputed question of jurisdiction.

senses.definition: To call upon someone for a favor, help, etc.
senses.example: I appeal to all of you to help the orphans.

senses.definition: To have recourse or resort to some physical means.
senses.example: When talks collapsed, some protesters began to appeal to violence to win their demands.

senses.definition: To be attractive.
senses.example: That idea appeals to me.

senses.definition: Of a fielding side; to ask an umpire for a decision on whether a batsman is out or not, usually by saying "How's that?" or "Howzat?".
senses.example: The bowler's teammates turned and appealed to the umpire, shouting How's that? after the close catch.

senses.definition: (historical) To accuse or charge (someone) with wrongdoing (especially treason).
senses.example: The king's officers appealed the nobleman of treason, accusing him of conspiring against the crown.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) Of a private person: to instituted legal proceedings (against another private person) for some heinous crime, demanding punishment for the particular injury suffered.
senses.example: The widow appealed her husband's killer of murder, demanding punishment for the loss she had suffered.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) Of the accomplice of a felon: to make an accusation at common law against (the felon).
senses.example: Hoping for leniency, the accomplice appealed the thief at common law for the robbery.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) To summon (someone) to defend their honor in a duel, or their innocence in a trial by combat; to challenge.
senses.example: Insulted at the banquet, the knight appealed his rival, demanding that they meet with swords at dawn.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The quality that makes something attractive or interesting to people; or a formal request to a higher court to reverse a decision.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PEEL, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak uh, not 'ah', and the word sounds like 'uh-peel', not 'a-pple'.

nuance.connotation: Positive in the everyday sense of attractiveness. Neutral in the legal sense, where it describes a formal process.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'appeal' most often to mean attractiveness, as in 'the appeal of living downtown' or 'it has broad appeal.' In news and courtrooms, it means a formal request for a higher court to reverse a ruling, as in 'file an appeal.' When you mean a plea for help, say 'an appeal for donations' in news language. A natural reply to 'What's the appeal?' is 'It's just so relaxing.'

distinctions.note: Attraction is neutral and general, while appeal often emphasizes a quality that draws people in and makes them want something.
A plea in court is a formal statement of guilty or not guilty, while an appeal asks a higher court to review and reverse a decision.
Charm refers to a personal, pleasant quality in a person, while appeal can describe either a person or a thing.

examples.everyday: The fried chicken has a lot of appeal, especially on a cold night like this.
examples.professional: The new dashboard has broad appeal with our managers, which is why we're rolling it out company-wide.
examples.analytical: The argument's appeal lies less in its logic than in its promise of moral certainty, which explains why it spreads so easily.

nuance.analogy: An appeal is like a magnet: it pulls people in without forcing them, though the strength of the pull depends on what they already want.
nuance.etymology: From Old French apeler, 'to call upon', from Latin appellare, 'to address, call to'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'appeal to' (to attract or to apply to a higher court) with 'appeal for' (to request help or money).
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, as in AP-eal, instead of uh-PEEL.

appeal.etymology: From Middle English *apel*, *appel* (“formal accusation brought in court; a challenge to trial by combat; an appeal to a higher court or authority; plea; pealing”), from Old French *apel* (“a call”), from *apeler* (“to call; to call out”), from Latin…

senses.definition: A respondent.
senses.example: After winning in the lower court, the appellee hoped she would win again in the appeals court.

core.definition: The party against whom an appeal is brought, who asks the higher court to uphold the lower court's decision.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, -LEE, not on the first syllable as in the dictionary's version. Keep the middle vowel reduced to a quick uh sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise legal role term with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use appellee almost only in legal settings such as court opinions, briefs, and conversations with lawyers. In everyday talk people say the other side or the party that won below. Pair it with appellant, the party who files the appeal.

distinctions.note: The appellant brings the appeal, while the appellee responds to it and defends the lower court's ruling.
Respondent is a broader term used in many kinds of proceedings, while appellee is specific to appeals.

examples.everyday: On that legal drama, the appellee's lawyer kept repeating the same argument.
examples.professional: Our legal team must file the appellee's brief by Friday to answer the appellant's claims.
examples.analytical: The appellee bears the practical burden of defending the judgment that the trial court reached.

nuance.analogy: The appellee is like the home team defending its scoreboard after the other side protests the result.
nuance.etymology: From Old French apeler, to call upon, from Latin appellare.
common_mistakes: Confusing appellee with appellant, the party who starts the appeal.
Stressing the first syllable as in the dictionary's version, instead of the last.

senses.definition: To be aware of perceiving; to understand a perception by linking it mentally with a mass of existing ideas of the same object.

core.definition: To become aware of a perception by mentally linking it with existing ideas, so that the new experience is understood in relation to what one already knows.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the final syllable, SEEV, which rhymes with leave. The middle vowel is reduced to a quick er sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise philosophical and psychological term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use apperceive mainly in philosophy of mind, psychology, and the history of ideas, especially in discussions of Leibniz and Herbart. In everyday speech people say notice, realize, or take in. Using it outside academic talk may sound affected.

distinctions.note: Perceive means to sense or notice something, while apperceive adds the step of linking the perception to prior ideas.
Realize is everyday and means to understand a fact, while apperceive is technical and refers to a mental process of interpreting.

examples.everyday: I didn't really apperceive how serious the problem was until my sister explained it.
examples.professional: The model should apperceive new user data by linking it to the patterns it already stores.
examples.analytical: Leibniz argued that we apperceive our own perceptions, making them conscious by attending to them.

nuance.analogy: To apperceive is like sorting a new letter into the right folder in a filing cabinet, so you understand where it fits.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ad, to, plus perceive, from percipere, to seize; the sense was developed by Leibniz and Herbart.
