nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use profitableness today. They prefer profitability for business and usefulness or value for everyday advantage. You may meet it in older writing or in careful academic prose, where it can sound a bit stiff in conversation.

distinctions.note: Profitability is the standard American term for capacity to earn a profit; profitableness is rarer and less natural in modern usage.
Usefulness refers to practical value in general, while profitableness specifically implies gain, usually financial or material.

examples.everyday: We talked about whether opening a second shop would be worth it, but nobody was sure about its profitableness.
examples.professional: The board asked for a clear account of the profitableness of each contract before renewing them.
examples.analytical: Medieval economic writers often judged an activity by its moral profitableness as well as its material gain.

nuance.analogy: Profitableness is the quality a field has when it produces a good harvest every season.
nuance.etymology: From profitable plus -ness, the suffix for a quality or state.
common_mistakes: Using profitableness when profitability is the more natural word in American business English.
Pronouncing the final syllables as separate vowels, such as 'bul-uh-ness', instead of a syllabic l.

senses.definition: Lengthy in duration; extended; protracted.
senses.example: The prolonged drought forced farmers to sell livestock earlier than planned.

core.definition: Continuing for a long time, or longer than expected or wanted; extended and drawn out.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -LONG-. The -ed ending is pronounced as a clear d sound after ng, so it is one syllable at the end, not an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in general, but often negative when it describes pain, silence, illness or waiting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prolonged for something long that goes beyond what was expected, such as a prolonged silence, a prolonged illness or a prolonged drought. It is more serious than long. In casual speech, people often say really long or drawn out instead.

distinctions.note: Long is neutral and everyday; prolonged emphasizes that the duration went beyond what was expected or wanted.
Extended often describes a planned increase in length, while prolonged often describes something that dragged on.

examples.everyday: After a prolonged wait at the DMV, I finally got my new license.
examples.professional: The project suffered from prolonged delays in the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Prolonged uncertainty can erode trust even when the eventual outcome turns out well.

nuance.analogy: A prolonged storm is one that keeps raging long after you expected it to pass.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of prolong, from Latin prolongare, to lengthen.
common_mistakes: Saying prolong-ed with an extra syllable instead of a final d sound after ng.
Using prolong as the adjective; prolong is the verb, and prolonged is the adjective.

senses.definition: An advancement in rank or position.
senses.example: I'll have to give myself a promotion!

senses.definition: Dissemination of information in order to increase its popularity.
senses.example: the promotion of the idea of global warming in schools

senses.definition: An event intended to increase the reach or image of a product or brand.
senses.example: The price cut is serving as a promotion of the manufacturer's new beverage varieties.

senses.definition: Transformation of a pawn into a piece (by reaching the opponent's back rank).
senses.example: When his pawn reached the eighth rank, the promotion gave him a queen.

senses.definition: Forward motion.
senses.example: The promotion of the sled down the icy hill was faster than anyone expected.

core.definition: A move to a higher job, rank, or position at work, or a marketing campaign that boosts sales or awareness of a product.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MOH. The final syllable -tion is pronounced as 'shun', with the vowel fully reduced, so avoid saying 'shun-ing' or 'pro-mo-tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Positive when it means a career advance; neutral when it means a marketing offer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use promotion most often for a job advance, as in 'She got a promotion.' In shopping, it means a sale or special offer, as in 'There's a promotion on coffee this week.' Context makes the sense clear, so listen for the setting.

distinctions.note: A raise is more money for the same job, while a promotion is a move to a new, higher-level position.
A sale lowers the price on a product, while a promotion can include gifts, bundles, or other special offers.

examples.everyday: She got a promotion at work, so she's taking us to dinner on Friday.
examples.professional: Her promotion to senior engineer comes with more budget authority and a bigger team.
examples.analytical: A promotion system that rewards visibility over output can distort what a team actually values.

nuance.analogy: A promotion is like climbing a staircase: you keep the same building but move to a higher floor with a better view.
nuance.etymology: From Latin promotio, 'a moving forward,' from promovere.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a promotion for a job' when you mean a job change; the correct phrase is 'a promotion to a job' or 'a promotion at work'.
Using promotion for a raise; Americans may say raise for pay increases only.

promotion.etymology: Late Middle English, from Old French *promocion*, from Late Latin *prōmotiō*, from Latin *prōmoveō* (“to move forward”).

senses.definition: A method of manipulating an artificial intelligence system by embedding malicious instructions (prompts) within input data in order to trick the model into overriding its intended behavior or safeguards.
senses.example: A customer's review contained hidden prompt injection that tried to make our support bot reveal account data.

senses.definition: A method of causing an artificial intelligence to ignore its initial instructions (often ethical restrictions) by directly giving it a particular prompt; a jailbreak.
senses.example: Users posted a clever prompt injection that persuaded the chatbot to ignore its safety rules.

core.definition: An attack in which hidden or malicious instructions are placed in input text to trick an AI system into ignoring its rules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word (PROMPT) and the -JEK- syllable of 'injection'. The i in 'in' is short, and the -tion ending is a reduced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: This term is used by security engineers, AI developers and journalists covering AI risks. Americans say 'prompt injection attack' or 'vulnerable to prompt injection' in security reports and meetings. It is not a casual phrase, but it appears often in tech news, so you may hear it in work conversations about AI safety.

distinctions.note: A jailbreak is a broader term for getting a model to bypass its safety rules, often by a user chatting with it directly; prompt injection specifically hides instructions in content the model reads, such as a web page or email.
Data poisoning corrupts a model's training data; prompt injection targets the model at runtime through its input.

examples.everyday: I read that a chatbot could be tricked by a hidden instruction on a website, which is a kind of prompt injection.
examples.professional: Our security review flagged prompt injection as the top risk for the document-summarizing assistant.
examples.analytical: Prompt injection exposes a deeper problem: a model cannot reliably separate trusted instructions from untrusted data in the same text stream.

nuance.analogy: It is like a forged note slipped into a stack of mail that a clerk follows as if it were a real order.
nuance.etymology: 'Injection' from Latin injectio, 'a throwing into'; 'prompt' see above.
common_mistakes: Saying 'prompt injection' as if it means a rapid shot of text; it refers to a security attack.
Stressing the second syllable of 'injection' as 'in-JEC-tion' with a long vowel; say 'in-JEK-shun'.

conversation.text: Prompt injection happens when untrusted text, like a web page or email, contains instructions the model then follows.
The agent reads customer emails, so prompt injection is our biggest security risk here.
There's no complete fix for prompt injection yet, so we limit what the agent is allowed to do.

senses.definition: Relating to prosecuting of criminal cases.
senses.example: Prosecutorial misconduct can lead to the lawyer's disbarment.

core.definition: Relating to a prosecutor or to the prosecution of criminal cases.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on TOR, the syllable before the -ee-ul ending, not on the first syllable. Keep the American r clear in TOR and don't turn the middle into 'kew'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but it often signals criticism: prosecutorial misconduct or prosecutorial overreach is a complaint about how a case was pursued.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in legal, courtroom and news contexts, usually with nouns like discretion, misconduct, power or overreach. You will hear it on the evening news or in discussions of a case more than in casual talk. In everyday speech, people more often say the prosecutor's office or the district attorney's office.

distinctions.note: A prosecutor is the person; prosecutorial describes something relating to that person or their work, as in prosecutorial discretion.
Judicial relates to judges and courts as a whole, while prosecutorial applies only to the side that brings criminal charges.

examples.everyday: My neighbor says the charges were dropped because of some prosecutorial mistake in the paperwork.
examples.professional: Our compliance team reviewed the prosecutorial discovery deadlines before the hearing next Tuesday.
examples.analytical: Prosecutorial discretion becomes hard to defend when charging decisions depend more on political pressure than on the evidence.

nuance.analogy: Think of the prosecutor as the offense in a trial: prosecutorial covers everything that offense does, from the charges it files to how hard it presses.
nuance.etymology: From prosecute, from Latin prosequi, 'to follow after, pursue'.
common_mistakes: Using prosecution as an adjective; say prosecutorial power when you mean the prosecutor's role, not prosecution power.
Stressing the first syllable; the word is pro-se-cu-TOR-ee-al, with the main stress on TOR.

senses.definition: (rare) Wantonness; waywardness; petulance; peevishness.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Stubborn, wanton willfulness; a petulant, perverse waywardness that refuses correction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TUR, the second syllable, which is an r-colored vowel. The final -ity is a light ih-tee, not a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes obstinate, almost childish defiance and is used in literary criticism or formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use protervity today, and when they do it is in literary or highly formal writing. In everyday speech they would say stubbornness or willfulness. Because it is so rare, it may puzzle listeners, so explain it or use a simpler word.

distinctions.note: Obstinacy is a plain, common word for stubbornness; protervity adds a sense of wantonness and petulance.
Perversity suggests deliberate contrariness, while protervity suggests a wayward, peevish defiance.

examples.everyday: My little nephew's protervity at dinner is legendary, since he refuses everything we offer.
examples.professional: The manager's protervity in meetings made it hard for the team to reach any decision.
examples.analytical: The novelist portrays the king's protervity as a kind of moral blindness that refuses every warning from his advisers.

nuance.analogy: Protervity is like a stubborn mule that plants its feet and refuses to move, even when the path is clear.
nuance.etymology: From Latin protervitas, from protervus, bold, wanton, from pro- forward and terere to rub or thrust.
common_mistakes: Confusing protervity with protector or protection because of the similar prefix.
Using protervity in casual speech, where stubbornness is more natural.

senses.definition: The prepending of phonemes at the beginning of a word without changing its morphological structure, as in Spanish esfera from Greek (via Latin) sphaera (“sphere”) (without prothesis the word would have become *sfera).
senses.example: Spanish speakers developed prothesis in words like escuela, adding a vowel before the initial s-cluster.

senses.definition: The preparation and preliminary oblation of the Eucharistic bread and wine in the Divine Liturgy of the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches.
senses.example: At the start of the Divine Liturgy, the priest performs the prothesis, preparing the bread and wine.

senses.definition: Credence table.
senses.example: Before the service, the sacristan placed the chalice and cruets on the prothesis beside the altar.

core.definition: In linguistics, the addition of a sound at the beginning of a word without changing its core structure, as in Spanish esfera.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PRAW, and the 'th' is voiceless as in 'thin.' The final syllable is a short 'sis,' not 'siss.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term used in linguistics and historical language study.
nuance.usage_note: Prothesis is mainly used in linguistics, historical phonology, and language study. In Eastern Orthodox liturgy it has a different meaning, the preparation of the bread and wine, so context matters. Americans rarely use it in everyday conversation, and they would describe the sound change in plain words instead.

distinctions.note: Prosthesis, pronounced PROS-thuh-sis, means an artificial body part, while prothesis is a linguistic term or a liturgical term.
Epenthesis adds a sound in the middle of a word, while prothesis adds a sound at the beginning.

examples.everyday: My Spanish teacher explained that the e at the start of 'escuela' is an example of prothesis.
examples.professional: The linguist's report flagged prothesis in the dataset, so the vowel onsets were coded separately.
examples.analytical: Prothesis in Spanish shows how a word's onset can change to satisfy phonotactic constraints without altering its morphology.

nuance.analogy: Prothesis is like adding a small step at the front of a stairway so people can climb it more easily, without changing the house behind it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek prothesis, 'a setting before,' from pro- 'before' and thesis 'placing.'
common_mistakes: Confusing prothesis with prosthesis, which is an artificial body part with a different stress pattern.
Using prothesis in a liturgical sense without context, when the word is used in several fields.

prothesis.etymology: From Late Latin *prothesis*, *prosthesis*, alteration from Ancient Greek *πρόσθεσις* (“addition, augmentation”), (English *prosthesis*) from *προστίθημι* (“to add”), from *πρός* (“towards”) + *τίθημι* (“to place”), from Proto-Indo-European **próti*,…

senses.definition: Closeness; the state of being near in space, time, or relationship.
senses.example: The proximity of the heat source allowed it to be detected by the sensor.

core.definition: The state of being near in space, time, or relationship; closeness to something or someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SIM. Don't pronounce the 'i' in the middle as a long 'ee' sound; it reduces to a short uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'proximity' mostly in formal writing, legal or official language, and more technical settings. In everyday speech they usually say 'closeness' or 'nearness' instead. It is common in phrases like 'in close proximity' and 'proximity to a school.'

distinctions.note: Closeness is the everyday word for physical or emotional nearness; proximity is more formal and often describes location or distance in a neutral, factual way.
Distance is the opposite emphasis: it measures how far apart things are, while proximity focuses on how near they are.

collocations: proximity of the house to the airport

examples.everyday: We bought the house mainly for its proximity to the grocery store and the park.
examples.professional: Because of the proximity of the two offices, the teams can meet in person whenever they need to.
examples.analytical: Proximity in moral life is not merely physical; relational proximity can create obligations that distance would not.

nuance.analogy: Like two houses on the same street: they are close enough to see each other's porch lights.
nuance.etymology: From Latin proximitas, 'nearness,' from proximus, 'nearest.'
common_mistakes: Using 'proximity' with 'of' instead of 'to' in phrases like 'proximity to the school.'
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, as in PROX-i-ty.

proximity.etymology: From Middle French *proximité*, from Latin *proximitas*, from *proximus*.

senses.definition: (archaic) Powerful, mighty, having authority.
senses.example: The puissant king summoned his lords to the hall and demanded their oaths of fealty.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Powerful, mighty or strong, especially in a formal or literary way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, PYOO. The middle syllable is reduced, so say it quickly as pyoo-uh-sunt, and the ending is -unt, not -ant.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes power or might, often with an admiring or heroic tone.
nuance.usage_note: Puissant is a rare, archaic or poetic word that Americans would recognize mainly from older literature, historical writing or fantasy novels. In normal speech use powerful, strong or mighty. Avoid it in everyday conversation, as it can sound affected.

distinctions.note: Powerful is the everyday term for having strength or influence; puissant is archaic or poetic.
Mighty is common in religious and literary language and emphasizes great size or force; puissant emphasizes power and authority.

examples.everyday: My grandmother used a word like puissant once, and everyone laughed because it sounded so old-fashioned.
examples.professional: In the proposal, I avoided puissant language and kept the claims concrete and measurable.
examples.analytical: The poem's puissant imagery presents the sovereign as a force of nature rather than a mere political authority.

nuance.analogy: A puissant ruler is like a mountain range: vast, old and impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Old French puissant, from Latin possens, being able, from posse, to be able.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as pwee-sant with a French nasal vowel; the usual American pronunciation is pyoo-uh-sunt.
Using puissant in casual speech, where it sounds archaic or affected.

puissant.etymology: From Middle English *puissaunt*, from Middle French *puissant*, *poissant*, Anglo-Norman *puissant*, Old French *pussant*, et al. present participle of *pooir* (“to be able”), ultimately from Latin *posse* (“be able”).

senses.definition: The act or an instance of puncturing.
senses.example: The puncture in the rear tire was too large to patch, so I bought a new one.

senses.definition: A hole, cut, or tear created by a sharp object.
senses.example: There were two small punctures in his arm where the snake's fangs had pierced the skin.

senses.definition: A hole in a vehicle's tire, causing the tire to deflate.
senses.example: On the way back we got a puncture, and we were stuck at the roadside for three hours until help arrived.

senses.definition: To pierce; to break through; to tear a hole.
senses.example: The needle punctured the balloon instantly.

senses.definition: To destroy the vitality or strength of.
senses.example: Years of cynicism began to puncture his hope for the company's future.

core.definition: A small hole made by a sharp object, especially one that causes a tire to lose air.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The vowel in pung is short, as in lung, and the final -ure is a rhotic reduced /ɚ/ that you should pronounce as a soft r sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it describes damage that causes failure or loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use puncture for a hole in a tire, which causes a flat tire, and say I got a flat when they mean the result. For skin, Americans say puncture wound or a puncture from a thorn. A sudden tire failure is a blowout, which is different from a puncture. Using puncture in casual talk is natural when explaining what caused a flat.

distinctions.note: A flat is the result, meaning the tire has lost air, while a puncture is the hole that caused it.
A blowout is a sudden, violent tire failure, while a puncture is a hole, often slow and gradual.
Leak means a slow escape of liquid or gas through any opening, while puncture specifically means a hole made by a sharp object.

examples.everyday: I got a puncture on the highway, so we're waiting for roadside help.
examples.professional: The vendor's packaging had a puncture, so we rejected the entire shipment for inspection.
examples.analytical: A puncture by a sharp object is a different failure mode from fatigue cracking, and engineers must diagnose each one separately.

nuance.analogy: Like a pinprick in a balloon, it lets the air out slowly until nothing is left.
nuance.etymology: From Latin punctura, from pungere (to prick).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as in pout or the ending as in bear.
Confusing puncture (the hole) with flat (the resulting loss of air), which Americans distinguish.

senses.definition: Purging.
senses.example: The purgative effect of the herbal tea left him weak and dehydrated all morning.

senses.definition: Something, such as a substance or medicine, that purges; laxative.

core.definition: A medicine or substance that empties the bowels; a laxative.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PUR. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so say guh, and the final syllable is a short tiv.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a clinical or historical term for a laxative, and it is used more often in medical or theological writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say laxative in everyday speech and at the pharmacy. Purgative appears in medical history, pharmacology and in theology, where it describes purification of the soul. In casual conversation it would sound odd for a bowel medicine.

distinctions.note: Laxative is the common everyday word; purgative is formal or technical and can suggest a stronger effect.
Purge is the verb to clean out or remove; purgative is the noun or adjective for a substance or process that cleanses.

examples.everyday: The doctor said I shouldn't take a strong purgative just because I'm feeling bloated.
examples.professional: The pharmacist checked whether the purgative would interact with the other medications on the list.
examples.analytical: Medieval writers often described penance as a purgative process that cleansed the soul of sin.

nuance.analogy: A purgative is like a drain cleaner for the body, clearing out what should not be there.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin purgativus, from Latin purgare, to cleanse.
common_mistakes: Using purgative in ordinary conversation where laxative is expected.
Confusing purgative with purgatory, which is a different word.

senses.definition: A coup d'état; an illegal effort to forcibly overthrow the current government.
senses.example: Afterward, the ringleaders of the failed putsch were publicly executed.

core.definition: A sudden, illegal attempt by a small group, often military, to seize power and overthrow a government.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short oo sound, like put, and it ends with ch. Americans often hear it as the German loanword, but it is a plain one-syllable word.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies an illegitimate, violent seizure of power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use putsch mainly in history and political news, usually about a failed or sudden attempt to take over a government. In everyday talk they say coup or coup attempt. The word is borrowed from German, so it sounds more academic than coup.

distinctions.note: Coup is the normal American word; putsch is mainly used for small, often military, attempts, especially in German or European history.
A revolution involves wide popular support and social change; a putsch is a small group seizing power.
A rebellion can be a large uprising against authority; a putsch is a sudden seizure of the capital or government.

examples.everyday: Did you hear about the failed putsch in that country last week?
examples.professional: Our analyst summarized the putsch as a small military faction trying to seize the ministry.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the putsch reflected popular discontent or only the ambition of a few officers.

nuance.analogy: A putsch is like a thief breaking into a house and grabbing the keys while the owners are asleep, rather than a long campaign to win the neighborhood's trust.
nuance.etymology: From German Putsch, a sudden blow or thrust, of imitative origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as pooch; the vowel is the short sound in put.
Using putsch for any political protest; it implies a forceful attempt to take control.

putsch.etymology: Borrowed from German *Putsch*, from *Putsch* (“knock, thrust, blow”), of origin.

senses.definition: One who quaffs.
senses.example: At the wedding, the uncle was an enthusiastic quaffer of champagne.

senses.definition: A quaffable wine.
senses.example: This crisp white is a quaffer, perfect for sipping on the patio all afternoon.

core.definition: A person who drinks heartily, often in large gulps, especially an alcoholic drink.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KWAH, and make the second syllable a quick, reduced 'fer'. The vowel is the same as in 'cot' in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful. It can suggest cheerful, hearty drinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use quaffer in everyday speech; it sounds old-fashioned or literary. In casual talk, people say 'drinker' or 'big drinker,' or describe someone's habit directly. You might see quaffer in a poem, a beer advertisement, or a historical text.

distinctions.note: Drinker is the everyday word; quaffer is literary and suggests drinking with enthusiasm and in large amounts.
A sipper drinks slowly in small amounts, the opposite of a quaffer.

examples.professional: The brewery's marketing targets casual quaffers at weekend festivals rather than serious beer experts.
examples.analytical: Medieval tavern songs often celebrate the quaffer as a figure of communal pleasure and generosity.

nuance.analogy: A quaffer is like someone who empties a glass in one happy swallow instead of savoring it slowly.
nuance.etymology: From quaff (verb) plus the agent suffix -er; the origin of quaff itself is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing quaffer with quaver, which means to tremble or a musical note.
Using quaffer in casual conversation, where 'drinker' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: In a queasy manner; delicately; squeamishly.
senses.example: She looked queasily at the spider crawling across the kitchen counter.

senses.definition: In a manner that makes one queasy; sickeningly, nauseatingly.
senses.example: The gray fog hung queasily over the marsh, making everyone on the ferry feel ill.

core.definition: In a way that feels sick to the stomach, or in a nervous, uneasy way that shows discomfort or disgust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KWEE, which rhymes with 'see'. The -ily ending is pronounced 'ih-lee', with the final y as 'ee'. Learners often add an extra syllable or pronounce the ea as 'eh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests sickness, nervousness, or disgust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use queasily to describe a person's manner, such as looking queasily at food or glancing queasily at a sudden hazard. It is mostly used in writing or descriptive speech. In casual talk Americans more often say 'I feel queasy' than use the adverb. The word can also describe an uneasy feeling about a situation.

distinctions.note: Nauseously describes causing nausea or being in a state of nausea, and is often criticized as a misuse. Queasily describes a manner that shows queasiness.
Uneasily describes general anxiety or discomfort. Queasily adds a physical sense of stomach upset or disgust.

examples.everyday: He ate the leftover sushi and then glanced queasily at the fridge.
examples.professional: The stock dropped queasily after the earnings call, and the team stopped talking about the roadmap.
examples.analytical: The narrator accepts the moral compromise only queasily, aware that his comfort depends on someone else's suffering.

nuance.analogy: Queasily is like a boat rocking gently in a harbor: the feeling is unsettled, and you never quite get your balance back.
nuance.etymology: From queasy (Middle English queisy, origin uncertain) with the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing queasily with nauseously, which Americans often treat as a misuse.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'zee' with stress, which shifts the rhythm.
Using queasily as a synonym for 'easily' because of the similar spelling.

senses.definition: The part that comes last or is situated in the rear; conclusion, wind-up.
senses.example: The rearward of the sermon brought everyone back to the simple message of grace.

senses.definition: The last troop; the rear of an army; a rear guard.
senses.example: The rearward of the column held off the ambush while the wagons crossed the river.

senses.definition: Toward the back or rear of something.
senses.example: The rearward seats of the bus were unpleasantly close to the toilet facilities.

senses.definition: Toward the back or rear of something.
senses.example: The mechanic leaned the seat rearward so the taller driver could reach the pedals.

core.definition: Toward the back or rear of something; located behind or moving backward.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, REAR. The final -ward is weak and sounds like 'werd,' not 'wahrd,' so do not pronounce the a as in 'father'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is precise and descriptive, with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly say 'back' or 'backward' in everyday speech. 'Rearward' appears in safety manuals, aviation, vehicle descriptions like 'rearward-facing car seat,' and military writing. It is correct in ordinary English, but in casual talk it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Backward is the everyday word for toward the back, and it can also mean slow to develop or going in the wrong direction; rearward is more precise and physical.
Aft is used in nautical and aviation contexts to mean toward the stern or tail, while rearward is a general term.

examples.everyday: Keep the baby's car seat rearward-facing until she is older, because it is safer for her neck.
examples.professional: The safety report flagged poor rearward visibility on the delivery van, which is why we added the sensors.
examples.analytical: The argument moves rearward through the text, tracing each claim back to the unstated premise that supports it.

nuance.analogy: Like a car backing out of a parking space, looking over its shoulder to see what is behind it.
nuance.etymology: From rear (the back part) and the suffix -ward (in the direction of).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'rear-WARD.' The stress belongs on REAR.
Using 'rearward' in casual speech where 'back' or 'backward' sounds more natural to Americans.

senses.definition: That reassures; causing or restoring comfort or confidence.
senses.example: The doctor's calm voice was reassuring, and the test results came back normal.

senses.definition: Reassurance.
senses.example: Her quiet reassuring during the power outage kept the kids from panicking.

core.definition: Making someone feel less worried, calmer or more confident about a situation or a person.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SHUR, the syllable with the r-colored vowel as in 'sure', and the first syllable 'ree' has a lighter secondary stress. Pronounce the r clearly; Americans say the r at the end of the stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes something that calms worry, and it is used both in everyday talk and in professional settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'reassuring' constantly in casual conversation, medical settings, customer service and workplace updates. It is a warm, friendly word, and people often say 'That's reassuring' as a response to good news. It is natural in both speech and writing.

distinctions.note: Comforting focuses on easing sadness or pain, while reassuring focuses on removing doubt or fear about a future outcome.
Encouraging means giving hope or motivation to continue an effort, while reassuring means making someone feel safe or certain about something.

examples.everyday: It's reassuring to know the kids are safe at their friend's house when it's storming outside.
examples.professional: The client sent a reassuring note confirming that the deadline will not change despite the server outage.
examples.analytical: The author's tone is reassuring, but a careful reader will notice that the evidence presented does not fully support its confident conclusions.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm hand on your shoulder before a nervous moment.
nuance.etymology: From reassure plus the adjective ending -ing, from Old French aseurer and Latin securus 'free from care'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'reassuring' with 'reassured', using the -ing form to describe a person who feels calm instead of the thing that causes the calm
Pronouncing the stressed syllable as 'sure' with a long oo sound in careless speech, which can sound unclear; keep the r sound clear

senses.definition: To baptize again.
To rename.
senses.example: After the fire destroyed the Bronx pub, it was rebaptized “The Bronx 2”.

core.definition: To baptize again, especially a person who was already baptized, usually because the earlier baptism is considered invalid or because the person has changed churches.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, TIZE, not on the middle syllable. Keep the short a in bap, and do not pronounce the first syllable as 'ree-BAP-tize'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theology, but sensitive in church settings: calling someone's baptism invalid can sound dismissive of their faith community.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in religious, academic or church contexts, such as discussions of Baptist or Anabaptist practice or of converts from other churches. In everyday talk, people would say be baptized again or get baptized a second time. The older sense, to rename, is rare and mostly literary, so do not use it for everyday renaming. If you are speaking with a religious person, avoid implying that their original baptism did not count, because many Christians find that offensive.

distinctions.note: Baptize is the basic act of administering baptism once; rebaptize adds the idea of doing it again.
Christen means to baptize and name a child, and in American English it is also used informally for the first use of something, such as christening a new boat.
Rebaptism is the noun for the act; rebaptize is the verb, so say the church will rebaptize new members, not the church will rebaptism them.

collocations: rebaptize someone who was baptized as an infant

examples.everyday: My neighbor decided to get rebaptized at the lake after she started attending a Baptist church.
examples.professional: Our denomination will not rebaptize anyone who was baptized in a Trinitarian church, so the new members only need a profession of faith.
examples.analytical: Augustine argued against rebaptizing the Donatists, holding that the validity of baptism depends on Christ rather than on the holiness of the minister.

nuance.analogy: Rebaptizing is like re-stamping a passport that is already valid: the first stamp still counts, so a second one is unnecessary.
nuance.etymology: From re- (again) and baptize, from Greek baptizein, 'to dip, immerse'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable (ree-BAP-tize) instead of the final syllable (ree-bap-TIZE).
Writing it with a hyphen as re-baptize in formal text; the standard spelling is rebaptize.
Using rebaptize for everyday renaming; in ordinary speech, rename or give a new name is clearer.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Greek New Testament the root word is baptizo, meaning 'to dip, immerse, wash'. The RSV does not use the word rebaptize, but several passages shape the debate. Ephesians 4:5 names 'one Lord, one faith, one baptism', which many read as a single baptism that is not repeated. Acts 19:1-7 describes disciples of John who were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, which many interpreters read as a distinct baptism rather than a repetition of a valid Christian one. Romans 6:3-4 says believers were baptized into Christ's death and raised to walk in newness of life, a passage often cited for the view that baptism is a single, decisive event.

traditions.view: Baptism is administered once and is not repeated. Those who come from churches whose baptism is recognized are generally received by chrismation, and only those whose baptism is doubtful are baptized.
Baptism imprints an indelible spiritual mark and is never repeated. When validity is uncertain, the Church gives conditional baptism, using words such as 'if you are not already baptized'.

Baptists and some other groups hold that only believers should be baptized, so they regard infant baptism as not true baptism and baptize adults. Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches generally recognize baptism performed in other churches and do not rebaptize.

senses.definition: The state of being receptive.
The extent to which something is receptive.
senses.example: The startup's receptivity to customer feedback helped it adapt quickly to the market.

core.definition: The quality of being open and willing to receive new ideas, feedback or experiences.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress falls on TIV, and the ending is '-ih-tee,' with a short i. Do not stress the first syllable, 'ree.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It names a quality of openness and is used thoughtfully in formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'receptivity' mainly in formal, academic or professional writing, often in phrases about receptivity to change or feedback. In casual talk, they usually say 'open to' or 'willingness.' In medicine it can describe the body's readiness to accept treatment.

distinctions.note: Openness is the more common everyday word, while receptivity sounds more formal and suggests readiness to accept something specific.
Receptiveness and receptivity mean nearly the same thing; receptivity is more common in academic and scientific writing.

examples.everyday: My sister has a lot of receptivity to advice, which makes her easy to work with.
examples.professional: The team's receptivity to the new workflow was higher than we expected after the pilot.
examples.analytical: Her philosophical receptivity to competing views made her argument more persuasive, since she clearly engaged the strongest objections.

nuance.analogy: Receptivity is like soil ready for seeds: it is prepared to take in what is planted.
nuance.etymology: From receptive plus the suffix -ity, 'state or quality of.'
common_mistakes: Stressing 're-sep' in the first syllable, as in 'REE-sep-TIV-ih-tee.' Actually stress is on the third syllable.
Using 'receptivity' in casual speech where 'open' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: To invigorate and revitalize one's energy level by removing stressful agents for a period of time.
senses.example: After a week at the lake cabin, I finally felt ready to recharge.

senses.definition: To charge an electric battery after its power has been consumed.
senses.example: Plug your phone in overnight to recharge the battery before the long flight.

senses.definition: To charge or accuse in return.
senses.example: When the reporter accused him of fraud, he quickly recharged with accusations against her.

senses.definition: To reload a gun with ammunition.
senses.example: The soldier had to recharge his rifle quickly before the next wave arrived.

senses.definition: To add or restore water to an aquifer.
senses.example: Heavy spring rains help recharge the aquifer that supplies wells across the valley.

senses.definition: To request payment again from.
senses.example: The collection agency tried to recharge the overdue account after the first notice bounced.

senses.definition: To attack again or anew.
senses.example: After the first assault failed, the general ordered his cavalry to recharge the enemy line.

senses.definition: The process of revitalizing one's energy level by removing stressful agents for a period of time.
senses.example: A long weekend of hiking is my favorite recharge after a stressful quarter at work.

senses.definition: The process of charging (an electrical device) again.
senses.example: My phone has needed five recharges in the last month.

senses.definition: Water that has percolated from the ground surface to an aquifer.
senses.example: The recharge from last winter's snowmelt replenished the aquifer beneath the farmland.

core.definition: To restore your energy, usually by resting or getting away from stress; or to charge a battery again.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, CHARJ. The 'r' is strong in American speech, and the 'ch' sounds like the 'ch' in 'chair.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests renewal and restored energy, and it is usually used with approval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say they need to recharge after a busy week or a long day of meetings, usually meaning they want rest or quiet time. For electronics, people say 'recharge my phone' or 'charge my phone,' and both are common. Saying 'I need to recharge' is natural and friendly.

distinctions.note: Charge is the basic word for adding electricity; recharge emphasizes doing it again after power has been used up.
Rest is any pause from activity; recharge specifically suggests regaining energy so you feel renewed.

examples.everyday: I'm going to take a long walk this weekend to recharge before the new semester starts.
examples.professional: Our team needs a short break after the release, so I'm asking everyone to recharge before next sprint planning.
examples.analytical: A person who recharges through solitude may be responding to the particular demands of social life rather than simply being tired.

nuance.analogy: Recharging is like filling a water bottle at a fountain after a long hike: you are restoring what you spent.
nuance.etymology: From re- (again) and charge, from Old French charger, 'to load.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'RE-charge,' which is a noun pattern rather than the verb.
Using recharge for a phone that has never been charged; it is used for restoring power that was used.

recharge.etymology: From Old French *rechargier*, from Old French *re-* + Old French *chargier*.

conversation.text: I just need a weekend away to recharge.
A walk outside helps me recharge after work.
I need to recharge my phone before we head out.

senses.definition: Capable of being, or qualified to be, recompensed.
senses.example: Because the injury was caused by negligence, the family's losses were recompensable under the policy.

core.definition: Able to be repaid or compensated, such as a loss, injury or service that deserves payment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, REK, with a lighter secondary stress on pen. The middle syllables are reduced to schwa, and the ending is pronounced -suh-bul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical or legal descriptor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'compensable' in legal and workplace settings, such as compensable injury under workers' compensation. 'Recompensable' is a rarer variant with the same meaning and sounds more formal or literary. In everyday talk, people would say 'paid for' or 'something you can get reimbursed for.'

distinctions.note: Compensable is the common American legal term for something that can be compensated; recompensable is a rarer variant with the same sense.
Reimbursable applies to specific costs that can be paid back, usually expenses; recompensable is broader and covers losses or services.

examples.everyday: My boss says the extra hours might be recompensable, so keep a log of them.
examples.professional: HR confirmed that mandatory training time is recompensable under our wage policy.
examples.analytical: Whether a moral debt is recompensable depends on whether the harm can be repaid in kind.

nuance.analogy: A recompensable loss is like a bill that the insurer agrees to pay back because the cause is covered.
nuance.etymology: From recompense, from Old French recompenser, from Latin recompensare 'to compensate', with the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Spelling it recompensible instead of recompensable, since -able is the standard suffix
Using it for expense repayment where 'reimbursable' is more natural

senses.definition: An item of information put into a temporary or permanent physical medium.
senses.example: The person had a record of the interview so she could review her notes.

senses.definition: Any instance of a physical medium on which information was put for the purpose of preserving it and making it available for future reference.
senses.example: We have no record of you making this payment to us.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of phonograph record (“a disc, usually made from vinyl, on which sound is recorded and may be replayed on a phonograph”).
senses.example: I still like records better than CDs.

senses.definition: A music album; broadly, any music released as a single, EP, etc.
senses.example: Their new record is full of warm folk songs about growing up in Ohio.

senses.definition: A set of data relating to a single individual or item.
senses.example: Pull up the record on John Smith. What's his medical history?

senses.definition: A data structure similar to a struct, in some programming languages such as C# and Java based on classes and designed for storing immutable data.
senses.example: Each order is stored as an immutable record with a timestamp and ID.

senses.definition: The most extreme known value of some variable, particularly that of an achievement in competitive events.
senses.example: The heat and humidity were both new records.

senses.definition: Enough to break previous records and set a new one; world-class; historic.
senses.example: The team posted a record profit this quarter, the best in company history.

senses.definition: To make a record of information.
senses.example: I wanted to record every detail of what happened, for the benefit of future generations.

senses.definition: To make an audio or video recording of.
senses.example: Within a week they had recorded both the song and the video for it.

senses.definition: To give legal status to by making an official public record.
senses.example: When the deed was recorded, we officially owned the house.

senses.definition: To fix in a medium, usually in a tangible medium.
senses.example: Please record the meeting minutes in the shared folder before Friday.

senses.definition: To make an audio, video, or multimedia recording.
senses.example: The band plans to record their next album in a studio in Nashville.

core.definition: To write down, store or capture information, sound or video so that it can be kept and referred to later.

pronunciation.tip: As a verb the stress falls on the second syllable, rih-KAWRD; as a noun it is REK-erd, stressed on the first syllable. Keep the r and the final d clear, and do not reduce the vowel to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when keeping an accurate account is useful, and it can sound official or legal in some contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use record for writing things down, saving audio or video, and official documentation, as in record a meeting or record a song. In everyday talk people often say take a video or save the voicemail, but record is standard when a formal account is needed. As a noun it is stressed on the first syllable, as in a world record or a medical record.

distinctions.note: To register is to officially enroll or sign up; to record is to capture information or events for future reference.
A note is a brief reminder; a record is a fuller, more permanent account that others can consult.
To document means to provide written or photographic evidence; to record can also mean capturing sound or video without written proof.

examples.everyday: Can you record tonight's show for me? I'll be at my sister's.
examples.professional: Please record all action items in the project tracker before we close the call.
examples.analytical: A good experiment must record every variable, or the findings cannot be checked by others.

nuance.analogy: Like a camera shutter that freezes a moment so you can look at it again later.
nuance.etymology: From Old French record, from Latin recordari 'to remember', from re- and cor 'heart'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the verb and the noun the same way; REK-erd is the noun and rih-KAWRD is the verb.
Using record for a quick, casual note, where note is more natural.

senses.definition: For, or relating to, recreation.
senses.example: The city built a new recreational center with a pool, gym, and climbing wall.

core.definition: Done in free time for fun and relaxation, rather than for work, study or medical treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -AY-, and the final -al is a reduced, quick 'ul' sound. Pronounce the -tion- part as 'shun', not 'shee-ohn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; recreational drugs carries a negative or legal sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use recreational constantly for leisure activities and equipment, such as a recreational vehicle or a recreational league. In legal and medical contexts, recreational drugs or recreational use means substances taken for fun rather than for treatment, and the phrase can sound negative. In sports talk, a rec league is an informal league for players who play for fun.

distinctions.note: Leisure is a noun for free time; recreational is an adjective describing things used or done in that time.
Entertaining means amusing to watch, while recreational means active and done for relaxation or exercise.

examples.everyday: We bought a used kayak for recreational paddling on the lake.
examples.professional: The resort's recreational facilities, including the pool and tennis courts, are open to all guests this season.
examples.analytical: A distinction between recreational and productive activity runs through much of modern economic thought.

nuance.analogy: Recreational time is like the margin on a page: it is not the text, but it gives the page room to breathe.
nuance.etymology: From recreation plus the adjective suffix -al, from Latin recreare, to renew.
common_mistakes: Using the noun recreation where the adjective is needed, as in recreation sports instead of recreational sports.
Stressing the -al ending instead of the -AY- syllable.

senses.definition: A shaky or unsteady gait.
senses.example: He walked out of the bar with a drunken reel that made everyone wince.

senses.definition: A lively dance originating in Scotland.
senses.example: She taught the children how to dance the reel at the Highland games.

senses.definition: A kind of spool, turning on an axis, on which yarn, threads, lines, or the like, are wound.
senses.example: a log reel

senses.definition: A device consisting of radial arms with horizontal stats, connected with a harvesting machine, for holding the stalks of grain in position to be cut by the knives.
senses.example: The combine's reel lifted the wheat stalks toward the cutting bar before they were severed.

senses.definition: A short compilation of sample film work used as a demonstrative resume in the entertainment industry.
senses.example: She sent a demo reel of her editing work to every studio in Los Angeles.

senses.definition: A chronological collection of pictures or short videos published by a user on an app or website and typically only available for a short period.
senses.example: She posted a reel of the hike on Instagram, and it got thousands of views overnight.

senses.definition: The music of this dance; often called a Scottish (or Scotch) reel.
senses.example: The band struck up a fast reel, and the fiddles soon had the whole room tapping.

senses.definition: To wind on a reel.
senses.example: He reeled the fishing line in slowly as the trout tugged against the hook.

senses.definition: To spin or revolve repeatedly.
senses.example: The carnival rides reeled and spun under the bright evening lights.

senses.definition: To unwind; to bring or acquire something by spinning or winding something else.
senses.example: He reeled off some tape from the roll and sealed the package.

senses.definition: To walk shakily or unsteadily; to stagger; move as if drunk or not in control of oneself.
senses.example: After three whiskeys, Dan reeled out of the bar and bumped into a parked car.

senses.definition: To back off, step away, or sway backwards unsteadily and suddenly.
senses.example: He reeled back from the punch.

senses.definition: To make or cause to reel.
senses.example: The sudden punch reeled him back against the lockers in the gym.

senses.definition: To have a whirling sensation; to be giddy.
senses.example: The sudden change in altitude made my head reel on the mountain road.

senses.definition: To be in shock.
To produce a mechanical insect-like song, as in grass warblers.
senses.example: At dusk, the grasshopper warbler began to reel from somewhere in the reeds.

senses.definition: To bring in or along.
senses.example: The new manager tried to reel in more customers with a loyalty program.

core.definition: To stagger or sway back and forth, often because you are dizzy, shocked, or drunk.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r clearly at the start and make the long ee vowel tense. The word has one syllable, so the stress is simply on the whole word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes unsteady movement, and can be used figuratively for a shocked mind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say the room reeled after bad news to describe a strong shock. In a literal sense, reel describes someone walking unsteadily, like after drinking. Reel is also a common word for the spool of a fishing rod or movie film, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Stagger means to walk unsteadily, often from weakness or drink; reel suggests more swaying or spinning and is often used figuratively for shock.
Wobble is a lighter, more physical shaking; reel suggests a stronger loss of balance or mind.

examples.everyday: I was so tired after the long flight that I was reeling when I got off the plane.
examples.professional: The team was reeling from the outage, so we paused the release until we understood the cause.
examples.analytical: The narrative reels between tragedy and comedy, so the reader never settles into a stable moral view.

nuance.analogy: To reel is like a ship in a storm, pitching so hard the deck seems to move under your feet.
common_mistakes: Confusing reel with real; reel is a verb about unsteadiness or spinning, while real is an adjective.
Using reel as a pronunciation match for real, leading to a shorter vowel; keep the vowel long.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the image of reeling is used for the staggering of people or the earth under God's judgment or distress. The Hebrew word behind it is nuaʿ (נוּעַ), meaning to totter, stagger, or shake. Psalm 107:27 describes sailors who reel and stagger like drunken men in a storm, and their helplessness leads them to cry out to the Lord. Isaiah 24:20 says the earth reels like a drunkard under the weight of judgment, showing how creation shakes when God's justice comes.

reel.etymology: From Middle English *reel*, *reele*, from Old English *rēol*, *hrēol*, from **hrehul*, from Proto-Germanic **hrehulaz*, **hrahilaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **krek-* (“to weave, beat”).

senses.definition: To bring (a fish etc.) out of the water by winding the line on which it is caught onto a reel (e.g. of a fishing rod).
To bring in (e.g. by attractive offers or persuasion); to lure.

core.definition: To wind a fishing line onto a reel to bring in a fish; also to attract someone with offers or charm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REEL, and in is short and unstressed. Link the words so it sounds close to REEL-in.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the fishing sense; in the persuasion sense it can sound manipulative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reel in for landing a fish and for attracting customers, clients or investors. 'Reel in a big bass' is literal; 'reel in clients with a discount' is figurative. The second sense can sound slightly manipulative, so use it with care when talking about people.

distinctions.note: Reel in pulls something toward you; reel off lists or recites things quickly.
Lure is the general word for attracting; reel in is more vivid and suggests gradually pulling someone toward you.

examples.everyday: I finally reeled in a bass after an hour at the lake.
examples.professional: Our sales team is trying to reel in mid-size clients with a free trial.
examples.analytical: The advertisement reels in consumers through emotion rather than evidence.

nuance.analogy: Reeling in is like pulling in a kite string hand over hand.
nuance.etymology: From reel, to wind on a spool, with the adverb in.
common_mistakes: Misplacing the particle; say reel it in or reel in the fish, not reel the in.
Confusing reel in with reel off, which means to recite quickly.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see reel,‎ off.
To list effortlessly and quickly.
To produce (e.g. a performance), in an effortless manner.
senses.example: The senator reeled off a list of statistics without consulting a single note.

core.definition: To recite or list things quickly and easily, often from memory.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REEL, and off is short and unstressed in the phrase. Keep the f clear at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests fluency, but it can imply rote memorization.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reel off for listing facts, numbers or names with ease, like a cashier reeling off the total or a student reeling off dates. It is informal to neutral; in a formal setting say recite or list. A natural reply is 'You really know your stuff.'

distinctions.note: Recite suggests saying a formal text aloud from memory; reel off stresses speed and ease.
Rattle off is very similar but sounds more rapid and casual.

examples.everyday: She reeled off the whole menu without looking at her notes.
examples.professional: In the sprint review, he reeled off the bug counts for every release.
examples.analytical: The philosopher reels off a list of objections, each stated quickly before he answers it.

nuance.analogy: Reeling off a list is like film unspooling from a reel, one item after another.
nuance.etymology: From reel, to wind, with off; the sense of rapid speech comes from unwinding a reel.
common_mistakes: Using it for physical movement; reel off is about speaking or listing.
Saying reel out, which sounds unnatural to American ears.

senses.definition: The process of refreshing; a means of restoring strength, energy or vigor.
senses.example: A cold lemonade on the porch was a welcome refreshment after the long hike.

senses.definition: That which refreshes, such as a light snack or drink.
senses.example: All refreshments will be provided by the hosts.

senses.definition: The result of being refreshed.
senses.example: The cool shower gave me a deep refreshment that lasted through the entire afternoon.

core.definition: Something, usually food or drink, that restores energy; often used in the plural for light snacks and drinks served at an event.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'fresh'. The middle syllable disappears, so the word has two syllables after the stress; do not add a vowel between 'sh' and 'm'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests comfort, hospitality and renewal.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, refreshments in the plural is the common term for light food and drinks at a meeting, party or event, as in 'Refreshments will be served at 3:00.' The singular is used more abstractly for a feeling of renewal. Americans might also say 'snacks' or 'something to drink' in casual talk.

distinctions.note: A snack is a small amount of food eaten between meals, while refreshments is a more formal term for food and drink offered at an event.
Restoration means returning something to its former state, while refreshment means regaining energy or a sense of renewal.

examples.everyday: There are refreshments in the lobby if you're thirsty before the show.
examples.professional: Refreshments will be served at the review, so please bring your questions for the team.
examples.analytical: Rest can be understood as a form of renewal, restoring the self rather than merely pausing work.

nuance.analogy: Like a glass of cold water after a long run: it restores what you lost.
nuance.etymology: From refresh, from Old French refreschement, meaning 'refreshing' or 'cooling', plus -ment.
common_mistakes: Using the singular refreshment when Americans usually say refreshments for food and drinks at an event.
Confusing refreshment, the noun, with refreshing, the adjective, as in 'a refreshing drink'.

refreshment.etymology: Recorded since 1665; either directly or via Middle English *refreschement*, from Old French *refrescher* (12th century; modern ), itself from *re-* (“again”) + *fresche* (“fresh”)

senses.definition: Without attention to; without regard for.
senses.example: He smoked cigars regardless of the consequences.

core.definition: Without paying attention to something; without considering its effect or importance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GAHRD. In normal speech 'of' reduces to 'uv,' so you do not need to pronounce it as a strong 'of.' Link the words smoothly, like 'ruh-GAHRD-lus-uv.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can signal determination, fairness, or indifference depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'regardless of' in workplaces, news, and everyday speech to say that something does not affect a decision. It is often followed by a noun, such as 'regardless of your background.' A common reply is simply 'Exactly' or 'Right,' especially when agreeing about a principle.

distinctions.note: 'Despite' focuses on an obstacle that still does not stop something, while 'regardless of' means that a factor is not considered at all.
'Irrespective of' is more formal and common in policy writing, while 'regardless of' is more natural in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: Regardless of the weather, we're meeting at noon by the fountain.
examples.professional: Regardless of team size, every sprint review should end with a working demo.
examples.analytical: Regardless of one's background, moral duties bind all rational agents equally, on this view.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls the same rules for every player, no matter who they are.
nuance.etymology: From regard (noun) plus -less, used as a preposition with 'of.'
common_mistakes: Dropping 'of' in formal writing: 'regardless the outcome' sounds informal; 'regardless of the outcome' is standard.
Using 'irregardless of' as a combined form; say 'regardless of' only.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the reign of a monarch (or pope).
Describing the year of a monarch's reign starting from the date of accession.
senses.example: The document was dated by regnal year, counting from the day the king took the throne.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a taxon at the rank of regnum (or kingdom).
senses.example: Biologists placed the fungi in their own regnal category, separate from plants and animals.

core.definition: Relating to the reign of a king, queen, or other monarch, such as dating events by a ruler's years in office.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, REG. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, and the ending sounds like 'nuhl,' not 'nal.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise historical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use regnal mainly in history, numismatics, museum labels, and genealogy. You will see 'regnal year' or 'regnal name' on coins, charters, and papal documents. In everyday conversation, people say 'the king's reign' or 'the year he came to power' instead.

distinctions.note: Royal describes anything belonging to a royal family; regnal specifically concerns a ruler's period of reign.
Reign is the period of rule itself; regnal is the adjective describing that period, especially for dating purposes.

examples.everyday: The museum guide said this coin is dated by regnal year, not by the calendar year.
examples.professional: The catalog lists each manuscript's regnal dating, which helps us place it within a specific decade.
examples.analytical: Medieval charters often use regnal years, tying a document's date to the sovereign's accession rather than to a universal calendar.

nuance.analogy: Regnal dating is like counting years from the day you got your first job rather than from the calendar's start.
nuance.etymology: From Latin regnum, meaning kingdom or rule.
common_mistakes: Confusing regnal with regional or regular.
Using regnal for modern government; the word applies to monarchs or popes.

senses.definition: That can be relocated.
senses.example: The data center uses relocatable servers that can be moved to another site in hours.

senses.definition: Movable, but not functional/usable while being transported.
senses.example: The radar unit is relocatable, but it must be shut down before the truck moves.

senses.definition: That functions identically at any address in memory.
A temporary building that can be dismantled and set up in another location.
senses.example: The school added two relocatables behind the gym to handle the enrollment surge.

core.definition: Able to be moved to a different place, or (in computing) able to run correctly at any memory address.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LOH, with a lighter secondary stress on the first syllable. Do not reduce the -ate- syllable to a weak vowel, and end with a light, unstressed -uh-buhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term, so it carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in software, hardware, and engineering contexts, such as relocatable code or a relocatable object file. For furniture or buildings, Americans more often say movable, portable, or prefabricated. In everyday talk, say can be moved instead.

distinctions.note: Portable means designed to be carried easily, like a laptop. Relocatable means it can be taken apart, moved, and set up again while still working correctly.
Movable is the general word for something that can be shifted. Relocatable is narrower and suggests a planned move to a new site or address.

examples.everyday: Our contractor said the storage shed is relocatable, so we can move it to the other side of the yard.
examples.professional: We compiled the library as relocatable code so it can be loaded at any address in the container image.
examples.analytical: A relocatable program is one whose correctness does not depend on the absolute position it occupies in memory, which is why it is a property of its references rather than its location.

nuance.analogy: A relocatable program is like a well-packed piece of furniture that fits any room because its parts refer to each other, not to the walls.
nuance.etymology: From relocate, from Latin re- (again) and locare (to place), from locus (place), plus the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (RE-lo-cat-able) instead of LOH.
Using relocatable to mean relocated, as in 'the office is relocatable' when you mean it has already moved.

senses.definition: Curative; providing a remedy.
senses.example: The surgeon prescribed remedial exercises to restore strength and mobility in his injured shoulder.

senses.definition: Intended to remediate (i.e. correct or improve) deficient skills in some subject.
A pupil enrolled in special classes to improve deficient skills.
senses.example: After falling behind in math, Danny was placed with the remedials for a semester.

core.definition: Designed to correct or improve skills or knowledge in which a student or worker is weak or deficient.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MEE, the second syllable. The final -ial is a reduced syllable, so it sounds like 'ul', and the first syllable is a weak 'rih'. The medical sense of 'curative' is rarer in American use.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but can sound slightly negative when applied to a person
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, remedial is most common in education, where a remedial class or remedial reading course helps students who are behind. Calling an adult 'remedial' in front of others is insulting, so speakers often say 'developmental' or 'support' instead. For a course, the phrase 'remedial math' is natural and neutral.

distinctions.note: Developmental is the more polite American term used by colleges, while remedial is more direct and can sound judgmental.
Corrective describes any action that fixes an error, while remedial specifically refers to making up for a deficiency in skills.

examples.everyday: My daughter is taking a remedial math class this summer so she can catch up before school starts.
examples.professional: The company offers remedial training for new hires who need help with spreadsheet basics.
examples.analytical: A remedial approach to moral formation treats vice as a deficiency to be corrected by practice and grace.

nuance.analogy: Remedial instruction is like physical therapy after an injury: it rebuilds a skill that was weakened so the person can rejoin normal activity.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin remedialis, from Latin remedium, 'remedy'.
common_mistakes: Using remedial to describe a person as dull, which is rude in American English.
Pronouncing it with the stress on the first syllable.

senses.definition: To change the appearance, layout, or furnishings of.
Synonym of remodeling.
senses.example: The remodel of our kitchen took three months and cost twice our original estimate.

core.definition: To change the layout, structure, or finishes of a building or room, usually to make it more modern or useful.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MOD, not on the first syllable. The final syllable is weak and sounds like 'duhl', with no full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a practical home or building project and carries no negative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'remodel' for changing the inside of a space, such as a kitchen or bathroom, and 'renovate' for larger work that restores or upgrades a building. 'Redo' is a casual alternative. People often say 'We're remodeling' when talking about a home project with a contractor.

distinctions.note: Renovate means to restore or modernize something to good condition, while remodel focuses on changing its layout or design.
Redecorate changes only paint, furniture, or decoration, but remodel changes walls, floors, or the structure.

examples.everyday: We're finally going to remodel the kitchen this summer.
examples.professional: The facilities team will remodel the third floor into open meeting space next quarter.
examples.analytical: The author does not simply remodel an old theory but rebuilds its foundations around new evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like moving the walls of a house while keeping the same address.
nuance.etymology: From re- 'again' plus model, from Italian modello 'measure, pattern'.
common_mistakes: Using 'remodel' for building a new house from scratch; for that, say 'build' or 'construct'.
Putting the stress on the first syllable, saying 'REE-mo-dul'.
Using 'remodel' for painting only; say 'redecorate' or 'repaint' for surface changes.

senses.definition: The act of repaying.
senses.example: Her repayment of the loan was completed ahead of schedule last spring.

senses.definition: The money or other item that is repaid.
senses.example: The monthly repayment of $350 covers both interest and principal on the car loan.

senses.definition: The act of revenge, an act of revenge.
senses.example: The mobster promised a bloody repayment for the betrayal, and everyone at the table knew it.

core.definition: Money or something else you give back to pay off a debt or to return a favor.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on PAY, and the final syllable -ment is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like 'ment' not 'mint'. Do not stress the -ment ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is used in business and finance without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use repayment mainly for loans, mortgages, and debts, as in 'monthly repayments.' In everyday speech people often say 'paying back' instead. In a sense of revenge, the word is rare and literary.

distinctions.note: Payment is any money paid for anything, while repayment specifically means paying back a debt or loan.
A refund is money returned to a customer, while a repayment is returning borrowed money.

examples.everyday: My car repayments are due on the first of every month.
examples.professional: The repayment schedule for the equipment financing starts in March.
examples.analytical: In the Bible, divine repayment is ultimately a matter of justice rather than human vengeance.

nuance.analogy: A repayment is like returning the change you owe after borrowing a twenty-dollar bill.
nuance.etymology: From repay plus the suffix -ment, meaning the act or result of repaying.
common_mistakes: Using repayment for a single purchase, when payment is the correct word.
Pronouncing the -ment ending as a full syllable rather than a reduced vowel.
nuance.biblical_note: The biblical idea of repayment appears mainly as God's justice, in which God repays each person according to deeds. Romans 12:19 (RSV) shows that God, not the believer, carries out the repayment for wrongs. The Greek word is apodidōmi, meaning to give back or render what is due.

senses.definition: The act or process of regulating again, or reversing deregulation.
senses.example: Voters debated whether reregulation of the airline industry would lower fares or simply raise costs.

core.definition: The act of imposing new rules on an industry or market that had been deregulated.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LAY, the third-to-last syllable of the main stem. The middle syllables are weak, so say 'reg-yuh' quickly with a reduced vowel, not 'reg-you-late'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a policy action and carries no clear praise or blame, although supporters and critics use it with different emotional tones.
nuance.usage_note: You will hear this word in news about banking, airlines, energy or telecom when a government reverses an earlier removal of rules. Americans usually say 'new rules' or 'stronger regulation' in casual talk, and reserve 'reregulation' for policy debate. The verb form is 'reregulate'.

distinctions.note: Regulation means any set of rules, while reregulation specifically means putting rules back after they had been removed.
Deregulation is the removal of rules; reregulation is the reversal of that removal, so the two are opposites in direction.

examples.everyday: After all those flight delays and fare hikes, a lot of people are honestly pushing for reregulation of the airlines.
examples.professional: The memo proposes partial reregulation of the lending market, reversing several of the 2018 rule changes.
examples.analytical: Reregulation raises the question of whether earlier deregulation failed because of poor design or merely because of weak enforcement.

nuance.analogy: Reregulation is like rebuilding a levee after a flood proves the first design was too weak.
nuance.etymology: Formed from re- (again) plus regulation, from Latin regulare, to regulate, based on regula, rule.
common_mistakes: Using 'reregulation' for any new rule; it specifically means reimposing rules that were earlier removed.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'ree-reg-yoo-LAY-shun' with a long u in the middle.
Forgetting that Americans say 'new regulation' or 'more regulation' in ordinary conversation.

senses.definition: An act or instance of rerunning; a repetition.
senses.example: The county ordered a rerun of the recount after officials found several ballots were miscounted.

senses.definition: A television program shown after its initial presentation, particularly many weeks after its initial presentation; a repeat.
senses.example: I'm not a fan of the new Simpsons episodes, but the old reruns have me in stitches, although I've seen them countless times.

senses.definition: Another printing run (impression; batch of copies of a given edition) of a book, cartoon, etc.
senses.example: The publisher's third rerun of the novel sold out within two weeks of its release.

senses.definition: A political candidate who holds the same political agenda or doctrine as a past or incumbent holder of a given political office.
senses.example: Critics called him a rerun of the old governor, offering the same tired promises and policies.

senses.definition: A second or subsequent run of a computer program.
senses.example: Each rerun of the algorithm takes several minutes.

senses.definition: To run again; to repeat.
senses.example: The coach had the team rerun the drill until every player got the timing right.

senses.definition: To broadcast (a television program etc.) again.
senses.example: They're still rerunning The Flintstones on this channel.

senses.definition: To be broadcast again.
senses.example: The network will rerun the finale on Sunday night before the new season starts.

senses.definition: To run (a race or other contest) again.
senses.example: rerun the election

senses.definition: To run (a computer program) again.
senses.example: Restart the computer and rerun the installation.

core.definition: A television program shown again after its first broadcast, often many weeks or years later.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, the stress falls on the first syllable, REE-run. As a verb, it moves to the second syllable, ree-RUN, so the stress shift tells Americans whether you mean the noun or the verb.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. A rerun suggests something old or not new, though it is also an ordinary part of TV life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'rerun' for TV shows, and also in conversation about a movie or a repeated event. Saying 'Is that a rerun?' to a friend when a show comes on is very natural. The word is also used figuratively for a repeated situation, often with a slightly tired tone.

distinctions.note: A repeat is a general word for anything done again; a rerun specifically refers to a broadcast or recording shown again.
A replay is usually a single moment or play shown again immediately during a game or broadcast, not a whole program shown again later.

examples.everyday: Do you want to watch something new, or is there a rerun of that cooking show on tonight?
examples.professional: Marketing wants to run a rerun of last year's ad campaign during the holiday season.
