examples.analytical: Sociologists describe a city with severe housing inequality as a tinderbox, where one incident can spark widespread unrest.

nuance.analogy: A tinderbox is like a pile of dry leaves in a fire pit: nothing happens until a spark lands on it.
nuance.etymology: From tinder, dry material for kindling, plus box; the box held the flint, steel and tinder for starting fires.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, tinder box, which is less standard.
Using it only for literal fire; in American speech it often describes tension or conflict.

senses.definition: In a tiresome manner; wearisomely.

core.definition: In a way that is annoying, boring or wearing, in the manner of something tiresome.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is reduced, and the final -ly is a light 'lee'. It has three syllables after the stressed one, so say it briskly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that is annoying or dull in a way that is hard to bear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'tiresomely' in everyday speech. It appears mainly in written criticism or literary description. In conversation, people would say 'annoyingly' or 'so boring.'

distinctions.note: Annoyingly is more common and more casual, and it describes irritation. Tiresomely suggests dullness and repetition as well.
Tediously focuses on boredom and slow length, and it is common in both speech and writing.

examples.everyday: The meeting dragged on tiresomely, and I wanted to scream.
examples.professional: The vendor's slides were tiresomely repetitive, so we skipped to the cost section.
examples.analytical: The essay argues tiresomely at points, returning to the same premise without advancing the thesis.

nuance.analogy: Speaking tiresomely is like a song played on repeat until it stops being pleasant.
nuance.etymology: From tiresome, plus the suffix -ly; tiresome is from tire, the verb, plus -some.
common_mistakes: Using 'tiresomely' in casual speech where 'annoyingly' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'tiredly,' which means in a way that shows you are tired.

senses.definition: Any physical device meant to ease or do a task.
senses.example: Several prehistoric tools, including a stone ax, were found during the dig.

senses.definition: Any piece of equipment used in a profession, such as a craftsman's.
senses.example: the tools of the trade

senses.definition: Anything that aids someone to perform an operation; an instrument; a means.
senses.example: Idleness is a tool of the devil.

senses.definition: A piece of software used to develop software or hardware, or to perform low-level operations.
senses.example: The software engineer had been developing lots of EDA tools.

senses.definition: A person or group which is used or controlled, usually unwittingly, by another person or group, a pawn.
senses.example: She was a tool of the pharmaceutical lobby.

senses.definition: A penis, notably with a sexual or erotic connotation.
senses.example: Coach warned the locker room prankster not to wave his tool around anymore.

senses.definition: An obnoxious or uptight person.
senses.example: He won't sell us tickets because it's 3:01, and they went off sale at 3. That guy's such a tool.

senses.definition: A handgun.
senses.example: The officer said the suspect had a tool tucked into his waistband during the stop.

senses.definition: A particular skill pertaining to baseball (such as hitting, running, etc.).
senses.example: a five-tool player

senses.definition: To work on or shape with tools, e.g. hand-tooled leather.
senses.example: He spent the winter tooling leather for saddles in his cold garage workshop.

senses.definition: To equip with tools.
senses.example: The startup tooled its data team with new cloud analytics software last quarter.

senses.definition: To work very hard.
senses.example: We tooled all weekend to finish the migration before Monday's product launch.

senses.definition: To put down another person (possibly in a subtle, hidden way), and in that way to use him or her to meet a goal.
senses.example: Dude, he's not your friend. He's just tooling you.

senses.definition: To intentionally attack the ball so that it deflects off a blocker out of bounds.
senses.example: Ray tooled the ball off the blocker's hands and out of bounds for the point.

senses.definition: To travel in a vehicle; to ride or drive.
senses.example: We tooled down Route 66 in his vintage convertible all summer long.

core.definition: A device or implement, often held in the hand, used to do a particular task. Also anything used as a means to achieve a result.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long, tense oo sound, like 'pool'. The final l is clear in American speech, not swallowed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting usefulness and practicality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tool' for hand tools, software, and any method that helps achieve a goal ('AI is a tool'). For electric household devices, people often say 'appliance', and for kitchen items, 'utensil' or 'gadget'. Natural replies to a request to borrow one are 'Sure, grab it from the garage' or 'I've got one you can use.'

distinctions.note: 'Instrument' is more precise, often used for scientific, medical, or musical devices, while 'tool' is more general and everyday.
'Equipment' refers to a whole collection of items used for an activity, while 'tool' is a single item.
'Utensil' is used for kitchen items like spoons and spatulas, while 'tool' is for hand-operated work implements.

collocations: the right tool for the job

examples.everyday: Can I borrow your drill? I need the right tool for hanging this shelf.
examples.professional: Our shared notebook is a useful tool for sharing code and results across the team.
examples.analytical: Language is a tool for thought, but it also shapes which thoughts are easy to have.

nuance.analogy: A tool is an extension of the hand, like a lever that multiplies the force you can apply.
nuance.etymology: Old English 'tōl', meaning an implement or instrument for work.
common_mistakes: Using 'tool' for household appliances like a toaster or washer; Americans usually say 'appliance'.
Using 'tool' as a countable noun without an article in phrases like 'a tool for analysis'; the article is needed.

tool.etymology: From Middle English *tool*, *tol*, from Old English *tōl* (“tool, implement, instrument”), perhaps borrowed from Old Norse *tól*, but at any rate ultimately from Proto-Germanic **tōlą* (“that which is used in preparation, tool”), from Proto-Indo-European…

senses.definition: To hunt for or locate; to search for; to find.
senses.example: I need to track down a computer so I can check my e-mails.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see track,‎ down.
senses.example: She'll track him down the mountain and catch him before long.

core.definition: To search until you find someone or something, often after a difficult or long effort.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'down', with a lighter secondary stress on 'track'. In casual speech, the words link together, sounding like 'tra-kuh-DOWN'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive or neutral when you find something, and can sound frustrated when it takes a long time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'track down' in everyday life for finding a person, a receipt, a file, or a bug. It is very natural in casual talk and at work. A natural reply after someone finds what you need is 'Nice, you found it!' or 'Thanks for tracking that down.'

distinctions.note: Find is general and can happen by chance, while track down implies an active search that took effort.
Locate is more formal and precise, often used for a place or position, while track down is more conversational.

examples.everyday: I finally tracked down the receipt in the glove box of my car.
examples.professional: Can you track down whoever owns the staging database before the release?
examples.analytical: Historians tracked down the letter's origin by comparing paper watermarks with archival records.

nuance.analogy: To track down something is like following footprints through the woods until you reach the animal you were looking for.
nuance.etymology: 'Track' comes from Old French trac, 'trail'; 'down' is the directional particle.
common_mistakes: Saying 'track down to' instead of simply 'track down' when the object follows.
Using 'tracked down' with the past tense incorrectly, such as 'tracking down' when you mean a completed action.

conversation.text: I finally tracked down the guy who sold me the car.
It took me weeks to track it down, but I found the book.

senses.definition: The state of being tractable or docile; docility; tractableness.

core.definition: The quality of being easy to control, manage or solve; in mathematics and computing, the ability to be solved efficiently.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BIL, the third syllable, not on the first. Give the final syllable a clear 'tee' sound, and reduce the middle syllables to quick, weak vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes something that can be handled or managed, and often praises it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tractability' mainly in academic, technical and formal writing, most often about problems in mathematics, computer science or AI. In everyday speech, Americans say 'easy to work with' or use the adjective 'tractable'. Among people, the word can describe someone who is cooperative and open to guidance, though it sounds stiff in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Docility describes an animal or person who is meek and easily led; tractability focuses on being workable or manageable for a task.
Solvability means a problem has a solution; tractability means the solution can be found in a reasonable amount of time or effort.

examples.everyday: The puppy's tractability made training much easier than I expected.
examples.professional: We chose a simpler model for its computational tractability, since the full version would take days to fit on our servers.
examples.analytical: Researchers often trade fidelity to reality for analytical tractability, accepting a simplified model because the full problem cannot be solved.

nuance.analogy: A tractable problem is like a trail that is clear enough to walk, while an intractable one is a jungle with no path through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tractabilis, from tractare 'to handle', a frequentative of trahere 'to draw'.
common_mistakes: Confusing tractability with tractor, which is a farm vehicle.
Putting the main stress on the first syllable, as in 'TRAK-tuh-bil-ih-tee'.

tractability.etymology: From Middle English *tractabilite*, from *tractable* + *-ite*, after Latin *tractābilitās*.

senses.definition: Synonym of pathfinder.
senses.example: Our guide was a trailblazer who knew every hidden canyon in the desert.

senses.definition: One who discovers or makes a new path or way through an untraversed region.
senses.example: Centuries ago, a trailblazer cut the first path through the dense Appalachian forest for settlers.

senses.definition: One who is the first to do something in a particular field; an innovator, a pioneer.
senses.example: She was a trailblazer in women's engineering, becoming the first female dean of the college.

core.definition: A person who is the first to do something in a field, opening the way for others to follow.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TRAIL, the first syllable, and the second part, 'blazer,' is unstressed. Do not say 'blay-ZER' as in the jacket 'blazer,' and the final r is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone for breaking barriers or leading change, often in social, scientific or business fields.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'trailblazer' to honor someone who was first in a role, such as the first woman to lead a company or a scientist who opened a new research area. It is common in news articles, speeches and award announcements. Saying 'You're a real trailblazer' is a warm compliment, and a natural reply is 'Thank you, I had great mentors.'

distinctions.note: 'Pioneer' is broader and can describe early settlers or early researchers, while 'trailblazer' often emphasizes breaking a social or professional barrier.
'Innovator' focuses on creating new ideas or products, while 'trailblazer' focuses on being first to enter a path that others then follow.

examples.everyday: My aunt was a trailblazer; she was the first woman in our town to become a county judge.
examples.professional: Maria was a trailblazer in our analytics group, building the first production model that other teams now reuse.
examples.analytical: Galileo can be read as a trailblazer of empirical method, opening a path that later scientists treated as a standard.

nuance.analogy: A trailblazer is like the hiker who cuts marks into the trees so that everyone who comes after can find the way.
nuance.etymology: From 'trail' and 'blaze,' where a blaze was a mark cut on a tree to show a new path through the forest.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, 'blay-ZER,' which sounds like the jacket 'blazer.'
Using it only for physical paths; in American English it usually refers to people leading social or professional change.

senses.definition: Beyond, spanning or crossing, or on or from the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.

core.definition: Crossing or spanning the Atlantic Ocean, or relating to travel, trade or relations between Europe and the Americas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAN, and the trans blends into tranz-uht with a reduced middle vowel. Americans write it as one word, so say the phrase as one smooth unit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, since it simply describes a geographic or commercial connection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually write it as one word, transatlantic, with no hyphen or space, and use it for flights, trade or relations across the ocean. In everyday talk, people often say across the Atlantic or European instead, though the adjective is common in news and business. It always refers specifically to the Atlantic Ocean.

distinctions.note: Intercontinental means between continents in general and does not name a specific ocean, while transatlantic refers specifically to the Atlantic.
International means between nations, while transatlantic is specific to crossing the Atlantic, as with flights or trade routes.

examples.everyday: I'm taking a transatlantic flight to see my family in London next month.
examples.professional: The transatlantic team meets at 8 a.m. Eastern, so we all have to shift our schedules.
examples.analytical: Historians debate how much transatlantic trade shaped the economic growth of both Europe and the Americas.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge spanning a river, transatlantic describes a link that connects two shores across a wide body of water.
nuance.etymology: From Latin trans (across) and Atlantic, from Greek Atlantikos, relating to Atlas.
common_mistakes: Writing it with a hyphen or a space; the American form is transatlantic.
Stressing the middle syllable; the main stress falls on LAN.

senses.definition: The act of conducting or carrying out (business, negotiations, plans).
senses.example: The transaction was made on Friday with the supplier.

senses.definition: A deal or business agreement. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
An exchange or trade, as of ideas, money, goods, etc. personal interaction.
senses.example: I made the transaction with the vendor as soon as she showed me the pearls.

senses.definition: The transfer of funds into, out of, or from an account.
An atomic operation; a message, data modification, or other procedure that is guaranteed to perform completely or not at all (e.g. a database transaction).
A record of the proceedings of a learned society.
A social interaction.

core.definition: A business deal, such as a sale, purchase or transfer of money or goods, or the act of completing one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZAK, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun, not tee-on. The ns sounds like nz before the stressed vowel, as in transact.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, since it simply names an exchange, though it sounds more formal than deal or sale.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transaction for any business exchange, from buying coffee to a bank transfer, in both casual and formal talk. In everyday speech, people often say payment, purchase or sale instead. In formal contexts such as banking, finance and law, transaction is standard, and in casual talk you might say deal.

distinctions.note: Deal is the more common everyday word for an agreement, while transaction is more neutral and often describes the mechanics of an exchange.
A sale always means something is sold to someone, while a transaction is wider and can include buying, transferring money or exchanging information.

examples.everyday: The cashier said the card transaction didn't go through, so I paid with cash.
examples.professional: The payment system flags any transaction over five thousand dollars for manual review.
examples.analytical: Marx argues that market transactions hide social relations behind the exchange of goods.

nuance.analogy: A transaction is like a handshake that seals a deal: each side gives something and receives something in return.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transactio, from transigere, to carry through or complete.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun transaction with the verb transact; say complete a transaction or transact business.
Stressing the first syllable; it is tranz-AK-shun.

transaction.etymology: Middle French *transaction*, from Old French *transaccion*, from Late Latin *transactio*.

senses.definition: Able to be transmuted.

core.definition: Able to be changed or converted from one form, substance or kind into another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MYOO, the second syllable, not the first. Say the middle as one syllable, myoo, and the ending as uh-buhl.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a potential for change and is used in science, philosophy and history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use transmutable outside scientific, philosophical or historical writing. In everyday talk you would say changeable, convertible or able to be turned into something else. It appears in discussions of chemical elements, alchemy and deep moral or social change.

distinctions.note: Convertible is everyday for things that can be exchanged or changed into money or another form, while transmutable suggests a deeper change of substance or kind.
Mutable means able to change in general; transmutable specifically means able to be turned into a different substance or kind.

examples.everyday: A good mechanic can turn an old junker into something almost new, so the car feels almost transmutable.
examples.professional: The consultant argued that our legacy code is transmutable into microservices if we first isolate each function.
examples.analytical: Medieval alchemists believed that base metals were transmutable into gold, a belief later abandoned as chemistry developed.

nuance.analogy: A transmutable substance is like clay on a potter's wheel: its shape can be completely remade, but it remains clay.
nuance.etymology: From Latin transmutare, to change across, from trans- and mutare, to change.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of MYOO.
Confusing transmutable, able to be changed, with immutable, which means unchangeable.

senses.definition: Accompaniments to a meal.
senses.example: Our Thanksgiving dinner included turkey, stuffing, and all the usual trimmings.

core.definition: Side dishes and extras served with a main course, especially at a traditional holiday dinner such as Thanksgiving.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce ng as one sound, not n plus g. The final z is voiced, so it sounds like TRIM-ingz.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a generous, festive, complete meal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say a roast turkey dinner comes with all the trimmings, meaning stuffing, gravy, cranberry sauce, and potatoes. The word is almost always plural and is used mostly in conversation about holiday meals. A natural reply to 'We'll have all the trimmings' is 'Sounds great, I'll bring the pie.'

distinctions.note: Sides is the everyday word for side dishes. Trimmings sounds more festive and traditional and suggests a full set of accompaniments.
A garnish is a small decorative item on the plate, while trimmings are substantial side dishes.
Toppings are placed on top of food, like cheese on pizza, while trimmings are served alongside the main dish.

examples.everyday: Grandma's roast turkey came with all the trimmings: stuffing, gravy, and cranberry sauce.
examples.professional: The catering proposal includes the main course and trimmings for two hundred guests.
examples.analytical: The menu's trimmings reveal how a meal can signal shared tradition as much as nutrition.

nuance.analogy: Like the frame around a painting, trimmings complete the main piece and make it look finished.
nuance.etymology: From the verb trim, in the older sense of decorating; the food sense developed from decorative extras.
common_mistakes: Using trimmings for the main dish; the word means the side dishes that accompany it.
Saying a trimming for one side dish; the word is almost always plural.

senses.definition: The act of truncating or shortening (for example, words are shortened to form blend words or portmanteaus).
senses.example: Linguists often study the truncation of words like info from information in everyday speech.

senses.definition: The removal of the least significant digits from a decimal number.
An operation in any dimension that cuts a regular polytope at its vertices, creating a new facet in place of each vertex.
senses.example: In geometry class, a truncation of a cube cuts off each corner and creates a new triangular face.

core.definition: The act of cutting off or shortening something, especially by removing its ending or least significant digits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, kay. The sh sound is one unit, and the final -ion is a weak shun, not a separate ee-on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use truncation in computing, mathematics and statistics to describe an operation that shortens or cuts data, such as truncation error. In general speech, people would say cutting or shortening. The word is most common in technical documents and academic writing.

distinctions.note: Rounding adjusts the last digit to the nearest value, while truncation just drops the digits after a chosen place.
An abbreviation is a shortened form of a word like Dr., while truncation is the general process of cutting something short.

examples.everyday: The phone bill shows the total with truncation at the cents, so it never quite matches my math.
examples.professional: The truncation error in our model is small, but it grows when we run the simulation for many steps.
examples.analytical: Truncation is a principled simplification, yet it introduces a bias that the analysis must acknowledge explicitly.

nuance.analogy: Truncation is like cutting the ends off a loaf of bread: the loaf is shorter, and some of its substance is simply gone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin truncatio, the act of cutting off, from truncare.
common_mistakes: Using truncation for rounding; the two are different operations with different results.
Stressing the last syllable; the stress is on kay.

truncation.etymology: From Late Latin *truncātiō*, from Latin *truncāre*, past participle *truncātus* (“to cut off”).

senses.definition: In a tuneless manner.

core.definition: In a way that lacks a pleasing melody, often by singing or playing off-key.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TOON. The last two syllables are light, so say 'lus-lee' with the final y sounding like ee.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly humorous. It describes singing that is off-key, often in a teasing way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word to describe off-key singing or whistling, usually in a light or joking tone. People often say it about themselves to be funny. In everyday talk, 'off-key' is more common than tunelessly.

distinctions.note: Off-key is the more common everyday phrase, while tunelessly is a slightly more formal or descriptive adverb.

examples.everyday: Dad was singing tunelessly in the car, but he was having a great time.
examples.professional: The demo track was recorded tunelessly, so we need a new vocal take before the launch.
examples.analytical: A hymn sung tunelessly can still express faith, though it loses much of its beauty for the congregation.

nuance.analogy: Singing tunelessly is like drawing a line with a shaky hand: the line is there, but it doesn't follow the intended curve.
nuance.etymology: From tuneless plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using tunelessly to describe a speaker's tone of voice; it applies only to melody and singing or playing music.

senses.definition: To suddenly change or reverse one's opinion, point of view, stated position, behavior, etc.
senses.example: You can't just turn around and say that it was all my fault.

senses.definition: To reverse an expected outcome (of a game, etc.), usually from a losing outcome to a winning one; to return (a business, department, etc.) to effectiveness, profitability, etc.
senses.example: The new management team has really turned the company around 180 degrees, and they expect a good profit next year.

senses.definition: To physically rotate (usually around a vertical axis) for a half turn (180 degrees), a whole turn (360 degrees), or an indefinite amount.
senses.example: At the end of the road, we turned around and walked back to the hotel.

senses.definition: To change drastically in a fundamental way, often for the better; to change to the opposite (opinion or position).
senses.example: She turned her position around and now she is in favor of the merger.

senses.definition: To convert (an agent) to work for one's own side.
senses.example: The detective hoped to turn around the informant who had been feeding secrets to the rival gang.

senses.definition: To consider from a different viewpoint.
senses.example: Let's turn that around and look at it from another angle.

senses.definition: (often with a unit of time) To produce; to output; to generate.
senses.example: We can turn around 500 units by next week.

core.definition: To rotate to face the other direction, or to change a bad situation so it becomes successful or improves.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'round,' and 'turn' is lightly stressed. The 'n' of 'turn' links into 'around,' so say it as 'turn-uh-ROWND' with a smooth flow.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it usually describes improvement or a change of direction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use turn around constantly in daily life, for physically turning and for business or personal improvement. You can say 'turn it around' for a situation, and 'turn around' is also used in travel, as in 'turn around and go back.' For an opinion change, say 'change one's mind,' which is common in conversation. Note that 'turnaround' is a noun for a recovery.

distinctions.note: Turn back emphasizes going back the way you came, while turn around can mean any change of direction or any improvement.
Reverse is more formal and technical, often used for vehicles or decisions, while turn around is everyday and conversational.

examples.everyday: Hey, you took a wrong turn, so you need to turn around at the next light.
examples.professional: We need to turn around this project before the client review on Friday.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the church can turn around its declining influence only by rethinking its public witness.

nuance.analogy: Turn around is like a ship changing course in the middle of the ocean, heading back toward the harbor.
nuance.etymology: Combines 'turn,' from Old English turnian, with 'around,' from Middle English.
common_mistakes: Placing a pronoun after the particle incorrectly; say 'turn it around' or 'turn around,' not 'turn around it.'
Writing 'turnaround' as a verb; it is a verb phrase 'turn around' and a noun 'turnaround.'

conversation.text: Turn around, I want to see the back of the dress.
We had to turn around because I forgot my phone.
The new coach really turned the team around.
Can you turn this report around by tomorrow?
We're going the wrong way. Turn around at the next driveway.
The new manager turned the store around in a year.

senses.definition: Each of the flashing lights on each side of a vehicle which is used to indicate the vehicle is moving left or right.
senses.example: The hazard lights turn on all the turn signals.

core.definition: The blinking light on each side of a vehicle that shows the driver is about to turn left or right.

pronunciation.tip: Compound nouns usually stress the first word, so say TURN SIG-nul, not turn SIG-nal. The final syllable is a reduced schwa, so 'nul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say turn signal or blinker for this light; indicator is the common British term, so it sounds foreign in an American car. You will hear 'Use your turn signal' from drivers and passengers. Forgetting to use it is a common complaint, so a driver who signals is usually appreciated.

distinctions.note: Blinker is the everyday American slang for the same light; turn signal is the standard and more polite term.
Hazard lights flash on all four corners to warn of danger; turn signals flash on one side to show direction.
Indicator is the common British term for this light; in American English say turn signal.

examples.everyday: You forgot to use your turn signal back there, so the guy behind you honked.
examples.professional: Our fleet telematics flags any vehicle where the turn signal is not activated before a lane change.
examples.analytical: A driver's turn signal serves as a public sign of intent, which makes the rule against silent lane changes a question of trust and coordination.

nuance.analogy: Like raising your hand in class before you speak: it tells others what you are about to do.
common_mistakes: Saying 'indicator' instead of 'turn signal' or 'blinker' when talking about an American car.
Stressing the second word, SIG-nal, instead of putting the main stress on TURN.

conversation.text: He changed lanes without using his turn signal.
Your turn signal is still on; you've been blinking for a mile.
My left turn signal is out, so I need a new bulb.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: To apply torsion along the length of the arm of (a person).
senses.example: The wrestler twisted his opponent's arm until the referee stopped the match.

senses.definition: To coerce, force, or cajole.
senses.example: They had to twist his arm, but they got him to join the project.

core.definition: To pressure or persuade someone strongly, often more than they want, to do something they were reluctant to do.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'twist' and 'arm' most strongly. 'Someone's' is usually reduced to 'SUM-wunz,' so the 'one' sound is weak and the final 's' is a 'z' sound.

nuance.connotation: Often neutral or playful when used about a friendly invitation; negative when it describes real pressure or coercion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in casual, friendly settings: 'You don't have to twist my arm' means 'Yes, I'd love to.' It can also mean real pressure, as in 'Her boss twisted her arm to join the committee.' The literal sense, physically twisting someone's arm, is rare and can sound like a threat.

distinctions.note: Pressure is a general word for influence; 'twist someone's arm' is more informal and implies that the person resisted.
Persuade is neutral and positive; 'twist someone's arm' suggests more effort or reluctance on the person's part.

collocations: you don't have to twist my arm

examples.everyday: Do you want another slice of pie? Oh, you don't have to twist my arm!
examples.professional: I didn't want to lead the audit, but my director really twisted my arm to take it on.
examples.analytical: Coercion differs from persuasion because it makes a person act when they would rather not, as when a company twists a regulator's arm.

nuance.analogy: Twisting someone's arm is like turning a door handle that the other person is holding: you push them to give in.
common_mistakes: Saying 'twist the arm of someone' with the word order reversed; the natural order is 'twist someone's arm.'
Using the phrase too seriously in a friendly setting, where it simply means 'I'm happy to do it.'

conversation.text: "Want another slice of pizza?" "Well, if you twist my arm."
I didn't want to go, but Lisa twisted my arm.
We had to twist the manager's arm to get the extra budget.

senses.definition: Typewritten material, especially such a copy of a manuscript.
A file containing a replay of commands typed into a terminal, which can then be automatically typed by a program later on.
senses.example: The script command allows you to make a typescript out of the current contents of your terminal.

senses.definition: To transcribe into typewritten form.
senses.example: Please typescript the handwritten notes from the 1962 sermons before the archive closes Friday.

core.definition: A typewritten copy of a document, especially an unpublished manuscript or original text.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'pt' at the end is quick, with no extra vowel between the p and the t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds scholarly or old-fashioned in modern writing.
nuance.usage_note: In modern American English, typescript is used mostly by editors, archivists, historians and publishers for a typed manuscript. In everyday writing people say draft, copy or printout. Capitalized TypeScript is also a programming language built on JavaScript, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A manuscript may be handwritten or typed. Typescript specifically means a typed version.
A transcript is a written copy of spoken words, such as a court record or interview.

examples.everyday: My grandmother kept a yellowed typescript of her wedding speech in a drawer.
examples.professional: Send the editor the final typescript by Friday, and keep a backup copy on your drive.
examples.analytical: Scholars compare the typescript with the printed edition to see how the author revised the argument.

nuance.analogy: A typescript is like a snapshot of a draft, frozen on paper before the printing press takes over.
nuance.etymology: From type and script, from Latin scriptum, meaning written.
common_mistakes: Confusing lowercase typescript with the programming language TypeScript, which is capitalized.
Using typescript as an everyday word for any printed copy; a printout or draft is more natural.

senses.definition: Of a book or document, not abridged, shortened, expurgated or condensed; complete.
senses.example: an unabridged dictionary

senses.definition: An unabridged publication, especially a reference work.
senses.example: I bought the unabridged for my dictionary-loving grandfather last Christmas.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of unabridged dictionary.

core.definition: Complete and not shortened, with no parts removed from the original text or recording.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BRIJD, and the -ridged ending is one syllable with a j sound, not an extra syllable. Keep the r rhotic, and don't say 'uh-BRID-jed.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually signals quality and completeness, especially for audiobooks, dictionaries and reference works.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often see unabridged on audiobooks, editions and dictionaries, where it tells buyers they are getting the full text. In everyday talk, people might say 'the full version' or 'the whole thing.' The noun 'unabridged' is often used in shorthand for an unabridged dictionary, as in 'Do we have the unabridged?'

distinctions.note: Complete means having all parts; unabridged specifically means not shortened from an earlier, longer version.
Uncut is common for films and sometimes means without edits for content; unabridged is used for books, recordings and reference works.

examples.everyday: I bought the unabridged audiobook, because I want the whole story, not the short version.
examples.professional: Please send me the unabridged report, since the summary leaves out the methodology.
examples.analytical: Any serious argument about Augustine must rely on the unabridged text rather than selective quotations.

nuance.analogy: Like a full-length film compared with a trailer: nothing has been cut away.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus abridged, from Old French abregier, from Latin abbreviare, to shorten.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it with an extra syllable, as in 'un-uh-BRID-jed.'
Using it to mean 'unfinished' or 'unlimited,' which changes the meaning.

senses.definition: The state of being unavailable.

core.definition: The state of not being accessible, present, or ready for use at a given time.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on BIL, the third-to-last syllable, and the final syllable -ty is pronounced 'tee'. The unstressed vowels are reduced to uh and ih, so do not pronounce every letter fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a state of not being accessible, though it can be negative when it causes a delay or problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun mostly in business, IT, and service contexts, such as system downtime or product shortages. In casual speech, people more often say 'it's not available' or 'they're not around'. The noun is more formal than the adjective unavailable.

distinctions.note: Unavailable is the adjective used for a person or thing that cannot be obtained or reached, while unavailability is the abstract noun for that state.
Downtime specifically means a period when a system is not working, while unavailability can describe any state of not being accessible.
Shortage means there is not enough of something, while unavailability means something cannot be accessed or obtained at that moment, even if the supply exists.

examples.everyday: The unavailability of that model is why I ended up buying a different phone.
examples.professional: The team reported a six-hour unavailability of the payment service, which triggered an incident review.
examples.analytical: Scholars treat the unavailability of primary sources as a central limit on any reconstruction of the period.

nuance.analogy: Like a store with the door locked during business hours, so the goods exist but cannot be reached.
nuance.etymology: From unavailable plus the suffix -ity, a noun-forming suffix from Latin -itas.
common_mistakes: Using the noun when the adjective is needed, such as writing 'The unavailability is' instead of 'The person is unavailable'.
Misplacing the stress as 'un-uh-VAY-luh-BIL-ity' rather than putting the main stress on BIL.

senses.definition: Not inclined toward either side in a matter under dispute.
senses.example: The senator remained uncommitted on the bill until she read the final amendments.

senses.definition: Not bound or pledged to a cause, party etc.
senses.example: Roughly a third of the delegates were still uncommitted when the convention opened.

senses.definition: Not yet written to disk and logged.
senses.example: Any uncommitted changes will be lost if you disconnect from the source control system.

core.definition: Not yet decided, or not pledged to supporting a particular side, candidate, plan, or course of action.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MIT, the third syllable, with a lighter stress on un-. The middle syllable kuh is a weak schwa, and the final -ed is a short, unstressed id.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; it can suggest a lack of loyalty or conviction in personal or political contexts, but it can also mean simply keeping options open.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uncommitted for voters who have not chosen a candidate, for team members who have not yet decided, or for someone who avoids long-term obligations. In politics, uncommitted voters and uncommitted delegates are common phrases. In casual talk you might say I'm still uncommitted about the trip. Be careful with a partner who wants a commitment, since uncommitted can sound like you are not serious.

distinctions.note: Undecided means you have not yet chosen; uncommitted adds that you have not bound yourself to a side, cause, or obligation.
Noncommittal describes a vague answer that avoids taking a position; uncommitted describes a person's status.
Uninvolved means not taking part in an activity; uncommitted means not bound to a side, though you may still participate.

examples.everyday: I'm still uncommitted about the weekend, so text me Friday and I'll let you know.
examples.professional: About twenty percent of the budget remains uncommitted, so we can fund the pilot if the review goes well.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's position is that an uncommitted skeptic keeps the question open, but this openness can slide into evasion if it never leads to judgment.

nuance.analogy: An uncommitted voter is like an open door: nothing is closed off yet, but no one is standing in the doorway either.
nuance.etymology: Un- (not) plus committed, from Latin committere, to join, entrust, or bring together.
common_mistakes: Confusing uncommitted with noncommittal; say I'm uncommitted about my plans, but give a noncommittal answer.
Using the wrong preposition: say uncommitted to a cause or uncommitted on the issue, not uncommitted for.

senses.definition: To set a price at less than the value or cost of an item.
To sell at a lower price than another (especially than a competitor).

core.definition: To set a price lower than the real value or cost of an item, or lower than a competitor's price.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, PRICE, with the first two syllables reduced. Don't confuse the word with overprice, which has the opposite meaning.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can describe a mistake or a deliberate strategy, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use underprice in business and marketing: a company underprices a product to win customers. In everyday speech they say 'priced too low' or 'sold it for less than it was worth.' The verb can suggest error, but it also describes deliberate strategies like low introductory pricing.

distinctions.note: Undercut means selling below a rival to take their customers; underprice can describe pricing too low even without any competitor.
Undervalue means judging something's worth as less than it really is; underprice means actually setting a lower price.

examples.everyday: The guy at the flea market underpriced his vintage lamp, so I bought it on the spot.
examples.professional: We underpriced the enterprise tier to win two big accounts, but our margins took a hit.
examples.analytical: A market that consistently underprices risk invites bubbles, since investors lose the signal that would otherwise restrain them.

nuance.analogy: Like selling bottled water for a dollar at a desert fair: you attract buyers but lose money on every sale.
nuance.etymology: From under plus price.
common_mistakes: Confusing underprice with undervalue when talking about people or their worth.
Stressing the first syllable; the main stress falls on PRICE.

senses.definition: Without making a mistake, perfectly, directly.
senses.example: His sense of direction leads us unerringly every time.

core.definition: In a way that is always correct or exactly on target, without making any mistake.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the ER syllable, and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech. The middle syllable -ing is short and quick, and the ending is 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises accuracy, skill or instinct, and suggests a near-perfect result.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unerringly in writing, speeches, sports commentary and descriptions of skill or intuition, such as 'she unerringly found the right answer'. It sounds literary in casual talk, where 'every time' or 'perfectly' is more natural. A natural reply to a compliment is simply 'You've got a good eye.'

distinctions.note: Infallibly stresses that error is impossible, often about an authority or doctrine, while unerringly describes accurate aim or judgment in action.
Accurately is neutral and measurable; unerringly carries a stronger sense of flawless, almost instinctive precision.

examples.everyday: My dad remembers every birthday and unerringly picks the right gift.
examples.professional: The model unerringly flagged the duplicate records in the test batch, so we trust it for the next release.
examples.analytical: Some writers describe the Scriptures as guiding the faithful unerringly toward truth, a claim theologians have debated for centuries.

nuance.analogy: Like an arrow that flies straight to the bull's-eye every time, with no wobble and no wasted motion.
nuance.etymology: From un- + erring; err comes from Latin errare, 'to wander, stray'.
common_mistakes: Using unerringly in casual speech where 'every time' sounds more natural.
Weakening the r in the middle syllable, which makes the word sound like 'un-AH-ing-lee'.

senses.definition: Having no guard or protection; vulnerable.
senses.example: The unguarded gatehouse was soon taken by the invading army.

senses.definition: Displaying a lack of caution or thought.
senses.example: I let out her secret in an unguarded moment.

core.definition: Not protected by guards or defenses; or, describing speech or behavior, careless and open, without caution.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on GUARD, and the u is a weak vowel. The word has no w sound, since guard is pronounced 'gahrd' in American English, and the -ed is a separate syllable 'id'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. An unguarded moment can be a positive candid moment or a negative lapse in caution, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'an unguarded moment' or 'an unguarded comment' to describe a time when someone let a true feeling or secret slip out. It is used both for physical places, such as an unguarded entrance, and for people. Saying someone was unguarded can be a compliment for honesty or a warning about carelessness.

distinctions.note: Defenseless means unable to defend oneself, while unguarded means not protected at that moment, often by choice or oversight.
Unprotected is broader and often technical, covering legal, physical or data protection, while unguarded often describes a momentary lapse in watchfulness.

collocations: let something slip in an unguarded moment

examples.everyday: He said he was disappointed with the job, which was an unguarded moment, but he was honest.
examples.professional: The server room door was left unguarded during the shift change, which is a serious security gap.
examples.analytical: Augustine's Confessions depicts the self in its unguarded moments, when desire reveals what the will has not yet disciplined.

nuance.analogy: Like a house with the front door left open while everyone is at the back.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus guarded, from guard, from Old French garder, 'to watch over'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing guard with a w sound, as in 'gwahrd'; in American English the u is silent.
Using unguarded to mean unaware in general; the word emphasizes a lack of protection or caution.

senses.definition: To cancel or withdraw an invitation.
A disinvitation.
senses.example: Her uninvite came by email just a day before the wedding.

core.definition: To cancel or withdraw an invitation that has already been given to someone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on VITE, the last syllable. The vowel in 'vite' is a long i, so it rhymes with 'bite', not with 'vit'. Keep the first two syllables light.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Uninviting someone is an unkind or awkward act, so it is usually done with an explanation or apology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say 'disinvite' for this act, though uninvite is also understood and used. It is used for events like parties, weddings, or speaking engagements when a host changes the guest list. Be careful: the act can cause hurt feelings, so people usually explain the reason gently.

distinctions.note: Disinvite is the more common American word for withdrawing an invitation, while uninvite is less common but still correct.
Cancel refers to canceling an event itself, while uninvite refers to removing one person from the guest list.

examples.everyday: My sister uninvited her ex from the party after she found out he was coming.
examples.professional: The conference board decided to uninvite the keynote speaker after the controversy, and they posted a short statement.
examples.analytical: To uninvite a person from a public event is to make a public judgment about their fitness to take part, which is why such decisions attract scrutiny.

nuance.analogy: Like taking back a dinner plate you already set on the table: the offer was placed, and now it is removed.
nuance.etymology: From un- + invite, from Latin invitare, to invite or summon.
common_mistakes: Using uninvite when Americans would say disinvite, which can sound slightly unnatural in everyday talk.
Using uninvite as a noun in place of uninvitation, which is the noun form.

senses.definition: Not distinguished on the basis of sex or gender; suitable for any sex or gender.
senses.example: Kim is a unisex name.

senses.definition: (dated) Of or pertaining to only one sex or gender; unisexual.
senses.example: Many plants have unisex flowers, so each blossom bears either stamens or pistils.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: The state of not being distinguished on the basis of sex or gender; the state of being suitable for any sex or gender.
senses.example: Critics argue that unisex has become a marketing buzzword rather than a real design principle.

core.definition: Not designed or intended for only one sex; suitable for both men and women.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the first syllable sounds like 'yoo', not 'oo'. The final 'x' is a clear /ks/ sound, so the word ends in a hard 'sex' rather than 'sexy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes products, spaces or services, and it can be positive when it signals inclusion, but some people use it dismissively for things that feel like compromises.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unisex for haircuts, clothing, fragrances, restrooms, and gyms, and the word is common in stores and advertising. Many people now prefer 'gender-neutral' for restrooms, names, and terms, because it sounds more inclusive. Avoid using unisex to describe a person's appearance, since 'androgynous' is the word for that.

distinctions.note: Androgynous describes a person's look or style that blends masculine and feminine traits, while unisex describes products or spaces meant for everyone.
Gender-neutral is the preferred term for names, restrooms, and language, while unisex is more often used for clothing, salons, and products.

examples.everyday: That salon downtown does unisex haircuts, so my husband and I can book the same appointment.
examples.professional: We chose a unisex uniform cut so the sizing works for everyone on the installation crew.
examples.analytical: The category of unisex products assumes that sex is irrelevant to the object's purpose, an assumption that deserves scrutiny when marketing relies on it.

nuance.analogy: Like a standard-issue sweatshirt designed to fit anyone who puts it on.
nuance.etymology: From uni- ('one') plus 'sex', formed in English in the twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Using unisex to describe a person's gender identity or appearance, where androgynous or gender-neutral is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable (uni-SEX) instead of the first (YOO-ni-sex).

senses.definition: A Christian theology that God is one person, rather than the three equal persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) posited by Trinitarianism.

core.definition: The Christian belief that God is one single person, rather than the three persons of the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'TAIR', and the '-ian' ending is 'ee-un', not 'ee-ahn'. The 'un-' at the beginning is a weak 'uh' sound, not 'oon'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly and religious studies; in some church settings it can sound like a theological objection.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, Unitarianism is discussed mainly in religious history and theology, and many Americans know it through the Unitarian Universalist Association, a liberal religious community that does not require a shared creed. Be careful: 'Unitarian' is the adjective and the noun for a believer, and 'Unitarianism' names the belief system. Most American churchgoers would not use the word in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: Trinitarianism holds that God is three co-equal persons in one essence, which is the opposite of Unitarian belief about the nature of God.
Unitarian Universalism is a modern American religious movement that merged two traditions and welcomes diverse beliefs, so it is not the same as the doctrine of Unitarianism.
Monotheism is the general belief in one God, which Jews, Christians, and Muslims all affirm, while Unitarianism is a specific Christian claim about the oneness of God's person.

examples.everyday: My neighbor goes to the Unitarian church downtown, but she says they don't really recite any creeds.
examples.professional: In the seminar, a student asked whether a Unitarian reading of John 17 could still be considered orthodox.
examples.analytical: Unitarianism denies the co-equal divinity of the Son and the Spirit, and therefore must explain Christ's worship in ways that Trinitarian theology does not require.

nuance.analogy: Like a monotheist who insists God is one, but declines to speak of that one God as three persons.
nuance.etymology: From Latin unitas ('oneness'), with the suffixes -arian and -ism.
common_mistakes: Confusing Unitarianism with Unitarian Universalism, which is a different and much broader religious community.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'yoo-nih-TAIR-ee-an-ism', which blurs the vowel in the -ian ending.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word echad means 'one' or 'united', and Greek heis also means 'one'. Deuteronomy 6:4 declares that the Lord our God is one Lord, a text Unitarians often cite. Matthew 28:19 instructs baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, a passage Trinitarians read as the basis of their doctrine. John 17:3 calls the Father 'the only true God', which Unitarians interpret as a claim about the Father alone, while Trinitarians read it together with the Son.

traditions.view: Eastern Orthodox theology defines God as one essence in three persons, as affirmed at Nicaea and Constantinople, and it treats Unitarian belief as a denial of this revealed truth.
The Roman Catholic Church teaches the Trinity as a defined dogma, and it considers Unitarian doctrine contrary to the faith professed in the ecumenical councils.

Most Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, and Pentecostal churches affirm the Nicene Trinity, although Unitarian churches grew out of sixteenth-century Protestant anti-Trinitarian movements and are regarded as outside historic orthodoxy.

senses.definition: The quality (as of a rule) of being able to be applied universally; that is, to any given situation with no exceptions.

core.definition: The quality of a moral rule or principle that can be consistently applied to every relevant situation, with no exceptions.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BIL, the third-from-last syllable, and the -ability ending is reduced to 'uh-bil-ih-tee'. Non-native speakers often stress the -iz- syllable or pronounce every vowel fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term in ethics and philosophy with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in academic philosophy, especially in discussions of Kant's categorical imperative and of John Rawls. In ordinary conversation people say 'consistent' or 'fair to everyone' instead. In a seminar or paper, it is the natural term for testing whether a rule could be applied to everyone without contradiction.

distinctions.note: Universality describes how widely something applies or is shared, while universalizability is specifically about whether a moral rule can coherently be applied to all cases.
Fairness is a broad everyday judgment about treating people equitably, whereas universalizability is a formal test of a maxim's logical consistency.

examples.everyday: My friend asked whether it was okay to skip the group project, and I said, 'If everyone did that, nothing would ever get done.'
examples.professional: Before we adopt the new data-retention rule, the ethics board wants to check its universalizability across all of our product teams.
examples.analytical: Kant's first formulation of the categorical imperative rests on the universalizability of the maxim, which asks whether it could be willed as a universal law without contradiction.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that works for every kitchen, not just the one where it was first written.
nuance.etymology: From Latin universus ('whole, entire') via universal, plus the suffixes -ize and -ability.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -iz- syllable instead of the -bil- syllable.
Confusing it with universality, which is about how widely something is shared rather than whether a rule can be consistently applied.

senses.definition: To remove a mask from someone.
To expose, or reveal the true character of someone.
To remove one's mask.
To cease engaging in masking, to cease disguising one's autism.
senses.example: After years of masking at school, she began to unmask and let her stims show.

senses.definition: To enable (an interrupt, etc.) by unsetting or setting the associated bit.
senses.example: Firmware must unmask the timer interrupt before the processor can respond to new events.

senses.definition: (dated) To expose something that was concealed or shielded from an enemy.
senses.example: The scout's report was meant to unmask the enemy's hidden artillery batteries before dawn.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To remove a mask or disguise from someone, or to reveal someone's true identity or real character.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on MASK, the second syllable. The s is a clear s before the k, and the a is the short a of 'cat', not 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context: it can mean exposing a fraud or a harmful revelation of someone's private life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in news, politics and everyday talk about hidden wrongdoing: 'unmasked as a fraud' or 'the reporter unmasked the scam'. The literal sense of removing a physical mask is less common, except at Halloween or in costume discussions. When someone reveals a secret, people often reply with 'Wait, really?'

distinctions.note: Expose is broader and often means revealing wrongdoing or facts; unmask focuses on removing a disguise or false identity.
Reveal is neutral and general; unmask implies that someone was hiding behind a false appearance.

examples.everyday: At the end of the show, the host finally unmasked the mystery guest, and the whole room cheered.
examples.professional: The security team unmasked the phishing account by tracing its login history back to a single IP address.
examples.analytical: Marx argued that ideology works by concealing class interests, and his critique aimed to unmask those interests beneath apparently neutral laws.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling back a stage curtain to show the machinery behind the magic show.
nuance.etymology: un- + mask; mask comes from French masque, from Italian maschera, 'disguise'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; it is un-MASK, with stress on the second syllable.
Using it simply for hiding something; the verb means removing a mask or revealing a hidden identity.

senses.definition: To remove the paving (especially in the form of paving stones, etc) from (a street); to cause to no longer be paved.

core.definition: To remove the paving, such as asphalt or paving stones, from a road, lot or path, so the surface is no longer paved.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PAYV, and make the final v voiced by letting your lower lip touch your upper teeth while you hum. Do not stress the first syllable 'un.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is usually used in urban planning, environmental work or construction.
nuance.usage_note: 'Unpave' is uncommon in everyday American speech, and people more often say 'tear up the pavement,' 'remove the asphalt' or 'take out the concrete.' You will hear it in discussions of stormwater, green infrastructure and urban planning, such as unpaving parking lots to let rain soak into the ground. In casual talk you could say 'they're tearing up the old lot to make a park.'

distinctions.note: 'Unpaved' is an adjective describing a surface that never had pavement, such as a dirt road, while 'unpave' is the action of removing existing pavement.
'Repave' means to put new pavement down again, while 'unpave' means taking the pavement away.
'Resurface' means to add a new top layer to a road, while 'unpave' removes the paved surface entirely.

examples.everyday: They're going to unpave that cracked lot next to my house and put in a little park.
examples.professional: Our stormwater team recommends unpaving the north parking lot to reduce runoff into the creek.
examples.analytical: Urban ecologists argue that to unpave a city block is to restore some of the soil's capacity to absorb rain.

nuance.analogy: To unpave a road is like peeling a bandage off a wound so the ground underneath can breathe and absorb water again.
nuance.etymology: From un- (reversing) plus pave, from Old French paver, from Latin pavire, 'to beat down, ram.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'unpave' with 'unpaved,' which is an adjective meaning a road that was never paved.
Using 'unpave' to mean 'to pave badly'; the prefix un- reverses the action, so it means removing pavement.

senses.definition: In an unreserved manner; showing emotion or lack of restraint.
senses.example: She unreservedly admitted that she had been wrong about the whole project.

senses.definition: Without reservation or shyness; readily.
senses.example: I apologize unreservedly.

core.definition: Completely and without holding anything back, often used to express full agreement or support.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZURVD, and the -ed ending is pronounced as /d/ before -ly. Say the final -ly as 'lee' and do not add an extra syllable between the d and the l.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses sincere, complete support, praise or apology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb in formal apologies, reviews, letters and professional praise, such as 'I unreservedly recommend.' In casual speech they say 'totally,' 'absolutely' or 'completely' instead. A natural reply to praise is 'Thanks, I really appreciate that.'

distinctions.note: Wholeheartedly stresses emotional warmth and enthusiasm, while unreservedly stresses that there are no conditions or limits.
Completely is a general, everyday intensifier, while unreservedly is more formal and carries the idea of no hesitation.
Unequivocally stresses that a statement is clear and cannot be misread, while unreservedly stresses full support without hesitation.

examples.everyday: I'd recommend that taco place unreservedly, because it's the best in town.
examples.professional: I unreservedly support the migration to the new data platform, and I think we should start next quarter.
examples.analytical: Mill argues that one can unreservedly accept a principle while still doubting how it applies to particular cases.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge built all the way across a river, unreservedly means there is no gap in the support.
nuance.etymology: From unreserved plus -ly, from un- plus reserved, from Latin reservare 'to keep back, save.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'unreservedly' (completely) with 'reservedly' (in a shy or cautious manner), which means the opposite.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of ZURVD in un-rih-ZURVD-lee.

senses.definition: Not sprinkled with seasoning.
senses.example: The boiled potatoes were unseasoned, so we added butter, salt, and pepper at the table.

senses.definition: Lacking experience.

core.definition: Not flavored with salt, pepper, herbs or spices; also, lacking experience in a role or activity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the SEE syllable. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, and the -ed ending is pronounced as a d sound after the z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing food; mildly negative when describing people as inexperienced.
nuance.usage_note: In restaurants and kitchens Americans use 'unseasoned' to ask for food without added salt or spice, often 'unseasoned fries' or 'unseasoned chicken.' For people, 'unseasoned' is a little formal and means inexperienced; 'green' or 'new' is more common in casual speech. A natural reply to 'Can you make the chicken unseasoned?' is 'Sure, I can do that, and I'll bring salt on the side.'

distinctions.note: Bland describes food that lacks flavor in general, often as a criticism; unseasoned simply means no seasoning has been added.
Inexperienced is a neutral, general term for lacking practice; unseasoned for a person is a bit more formal and suggests they have not yet been tested.
Green is informal and common in American workplaces for new workers; unseasoned is more literary and less casual.

examples.everyday: Could you leave the steak unseasoned? I'll add my own salt at the table.
examples.professional: Our unseasoned junior developers need pairing sessions before they touch production code.
examples.analytical: A newly appointed judge who is still unseasoned may apply the letter of the law too rigidly because he has not yet learned its exceptions.

nuance.analogy: An unseasoned person is like a dish with no salt: it has all the right ingredients, but it has not yet been tasted and shaped by experience.
nuance.etymology: From un- and seasoned, from season, from Old French seison, a time or period.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'unseasoned' with 'unseasonal', which refers to timing or weather, not food or experience.
Using 'unseasoned' to mean 'bland' in a complaint; for food that is boring, say 'bland' instead.

senses.definition: To remove shackles from someone or something.
senses.example: The captain ordered that the guards unshackle and release the prisoner, as he had served his sentence.

senses.definition: To remove restrictions or inhibitions; to allow full freedom and power.
senses.example: The new CEO unshackled the engineers from rigid approval rules so they could experiment freely.

core.definition: To free someone or something from shackles, chains or restrictions that hold them back.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on SHACK, and the first syllable is a reduced 'uhn', not 'un' as in 'fun'. The final -le is a syllabic 'l' with a light vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests liberation from something that held someone or something back.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unshackle mostly in writing, speeches and news about freeing people, economies or ideas, not in everyday chat. In casual talk, people say free or free up instead. It often appears with 'from', as in 'unshackled from debt'.

distinctions.note: Free is the everyday word for release; unshackle emphasizes removing the restraints that tied someone down, often in a more dramatic sense.
Liberate is more political and formal, often used for oppression or occupation; unshackle can be literal or metaphorical in personal or economic contexts.
Release means to let go or set free from a place or obligation; unshackle focuses on removing the restraints themselves.

examples.everyday: Quitting that job finally unshackled me from the stress I had been carrying for years.
examples.professional: The new rules unshackle our engineers from the old approval queue, so they can ship fixes the same day.
examples.analytical: Mill argues that individual liberty is needed to unshackle people from custom and the pressure of public opinion.

nuance.analogy: Unshackling is like unlocking a bike that has been chained to a pole for weeks: it can finally roll wherever it wants.
nuance.etymology: From un- (reversal) plus shackle, from Old English scacul, 'fetter'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'unshackle the chains' as a redundant phrase; the verb already means removing the shackles.
Using it for minor limits in everyday speech; say free up or loosen up instead.

senses.definition: Not stable.
senses.example: unstable foundation

senses.definition: Having a strong tendency to change.
senses.example: The stock market has been extremely unstable since the government announced its new tariffs.

senses.definition: Fluctuating; not constant.
senses.example: politically unstable

senses.definition: Fickle.
senses.example: He is unstable in his loyalties, dropping friends the moment they disagree with him.

senses.definition: Unpredictable.
senses.example: The weather on the mountain is unstable, so we checked the forecast twice before hiking.

senses.definition: Readily decomposable.
senses.example: chemically unstable

senses.definition: Radioactive, especially with a short half-life.
senses.example: Scientists sealed the unstable isotope in lead to prevent any leakage during transport.

senses.definition: To release (an animal) from a stable.
senses.example: Before sunrise, he unstabled the horses and led them down to the river.

core.definition: Not firm or steady; likely to change suddenly, shake or fail, such as a person's mood, a structure, a market or a situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAY, and the final -able is a reduced syllable pronounced 'bul', not 'bell' or 'bull'. Do not stress the un- prefix.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, implying danger, weakness or unpredictability; neutral in technical contexts such as unstable isotopes.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unstable constantly for weather, prices, relationships, moods and buildings. For a wobbly ladder they may say wobbly, and in news they often choose volatile for fast-moving markets. A common reply to 'the ladder looks unstable' is 'Good point, let's get a steadier one.'

distinctions.note: Volatile stresses rapid and sometimes explosive change; unstable can describe a steady but weak or shaky state.
Unsteady usually describes a person's balance or hand; unstable is broader and covers structures, systems and situations.

examples.everyday: The weather has been so unstable this week that I never know whether to bring an umbrella.
examples.professional: The forecast model became unstable whenever we added the noisy features, so we dropped them.
examples.analytical: A theory built on unstable premises will collapse as soon as those premises are tested against new evidence.

nuance.analogy: A tower of blocks that topples at the slightest bump.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus stable, from Latin stabilis, firm, from stare, to stand.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'un-stuh-BULL'
Confusing unstable with unsteady when talking about a person's balance

senses.definition: Not viable: not capable of independent life; not practicable.

core.definition: Unable to survive or succeed on its own; impractical or unworkable as a plan, business or living thing.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VY, and the final -able is a weak syllable, so say it as 'uh-bul'. Non-native speakers often give the first syllable too much weight or pronounce the middle vowel as a clear 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals that something cannot survive or work as planned, often a verdict on a plan, company or proposal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in business news, economics, medicine and biology, where it sounds precise and a little formal. In everyday talk people usually say 'not workable', 'won't work' or 'not going to fly'. Its opposite, 'viable', is much more common in conversation.

distinctions.note: Impractical means hard to use or carry out in daily life; unviable is stronger and means the thing cannot survive or succeed at all.
Nonviable is the same in meaning and is common in medical and biological writing; unviable is slightly more frequent in general business and news English.

examples.everyday: Honestly, driving to the coast every weekend is unviable with our budget right now.
examples.professional: The cost projections show that the new warehouse is commercially unviable without a major increase in volume.
examples.analytical: A theory that cannot account for any observable data is not merely incomplete but, in the relevant sense, unviable.

nuance.analogy: Like a seed planted on bare rock: it may germinate, but it cannot take root and live.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus viable, from French viable, from Latin vita 'life'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as UN-vy-uh-bul instead of un-VY-uh-bul.
Using it for a person who is simply weak; it describes plans, projects or living things that cannot survive.

senses.definition: Reproachful; chiding; censorious.
senses.example: She gave him an upbraiding look over her reading glasses.

senses.definition: An instance of severe criticism or rebuke.
senses.example: He received an upbraiding from his manager after missing the deadline.

core.definition: A harsh scolding or reproach directed at someone for a fault or mistake.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on UP, with a weaker secondary stress on 'brayd'. The final '-ing' is short and light, not a strong 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies sharp, sometimes public, disapproval from someone with authority or emotional closeness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely say 'upbraiding' in conversation; it appears in literature, sermons, news writing and formal analysis. In everyday speech, people say 'scolding', 'chewing out' (informal) or 'dressing down' (more formal). Use 'upbraiding' when you want to describe a stern, serious rebuke.

distinctions.note: Scolding is ordinary, everyday criticism, often of children or pets; upbraiding implies a sharper, more formal rebuke.
A reprimand is usually an official warning in a workplace or military setting; upbraiding is personal and more emotional.

examples.everyday: After he came home late again, his mother gave him a long upbraiding about the car and the curfew.
examples.professional: The manager's public upbraiding of the team embarrassed everyone and did nothing to improve morale.
examples.analytical: Job's friends offer a theology of retribution, and their upbraiding of him rests on the assumption that suffering must reflect sin.

nuance.analogy: Like a bell rung loudly over someone's head: it is meant to be heard by everyone and to make them feel small.
nuance.etymology: From the verb upbraid, Middle English upbreiden, to reproach, of Old English origin.
common_mistakes: Confusing upbraid with upbringing or upbeat; the words are unrelated in meaning.
Writing 'upbraid someone of something'; the standard pattern is 'upbraid someone for something'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind upbraid in the RSV is oneidizo (ὀνειδίζω), to reproach or revile. In Matthew 11:20 (RSV), Jesus begins to rebuke the towns where most of his mighty works were done because they did not repent. In Mark 16:14 (RSV), he rebukes the eleven disciples for their unbelief and hardness of heart.

senses.definition: Written in upper case; capital.
To convert (text) to upper case.

core.definition: Written in capital letters such as A, B or C, rather than small letters such as a, b or c.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, UP, and make the middle syllable weak. The word ends with the same sound as 'case' in 'face,' so do not say 'kus.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical technical term in typing, computing and printing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people often say capital letters or all caps, and uppercase is more common in technical writing, computing and typing. Typing in all caps can seem like shouting in online messages. Use lowercase for the opposite.

distinctions.note: Capital letters is the everyday phrase; uppercase is more technical and is common in software and typing.
Capitalize means to write only the first letter as a capital; uppercase means to write the whole word in capitals.
All caps is an informal phrase, often used online, and can suggest shouting.

examples.everyday: Please write your last name in uppercase on the form so they can read it easily.
examples.professional: The API expects country codes in uppercase, so convert them before sending the request.
examples.analytical: Case sensitivity means that a password in uppercase letters is a different string from its lowercase version.

nuance.analogy: Uppercase letters are like a name badge written in block capitals: bold, clear and easy to read from across the room.
nuance.etymology: From the printer's upper case, the tray that held capital letters, as opposed to the lower case for small letters.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words in technical contexts, where uppercase is the standard single word.
Using uppercase as an everyday word where capital letters sounds more natural to most Americans.

senses.definition: One who upsets (something); a disrupter.
A person or device that turns something upside down.
A kind of forging machine that moves horizontally.

core.definition: A person or team that unexpectedly defeats a stronger opponent or disrupts an established situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, UP, even though the verb 'upset' stresses the second syllable. The final -er is a weak, rhotic 'uh', not a full 'air' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it describes an underdog; negative when it describes someone who disrupts plans or peace.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'upsetter' in sports, such as a college team that beats a top-ranked opponent in March. It also appears in politics and business about a challenger or new company that disturbs established players. Many Americans would instead say 'giant killer' or 'spoiler' in sports and politics.

distinctions.note: An upstart is seen as arrogant or presumptuous, while an upsetter may simply be a successful underdog.
A spoiler is a candidate or player who prevents another from winning, often without any hope of winning.
Disrupter is common in business and technology talk and suggests changing an industry's basic model.

examples.everyday: That little school is a real upsetter; they beat the top seed last night.
examples.professional: The startup is an upsetter in the payments market, undercutting incumbents on fees.
examples.analytical: Schumpeter's idea of creative destruction casts the entrepreneur as an upsetter of established economic arrangements.

nuance.analogy: Like a small bird that knocks a heavyweight off balance.
nuance.etymology: From upset plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'upsetter' with 'upstart', which carries a negative sense of arrogance.
Using 'upsetter' to mean the upset itself; the noun for the event is 'upset'.
